The central musical fact of his career is the collaboration with the composer Bernard Herrmann, which ran from The Trouble with Harry in 1955 through Marnie in 1964 and produced some of the most influential film music ever written. Herrmann, who had scored Citizen Kane, was a master of short obsessive cells rather than hummable tunes, and his method suited Hitchcock's cinema of fixation perfectly. For Vertigo he wrote spiraling arpeggios that circle without resolving, music that is itself dizzy, and a love theme that openly echoes Wagner's Tristan, scoring the film's necrophiliac romance as ecstatic doom. For North by Northwest he wrote a careening fandango that keeps the picture's tongue visibly in its cheek. And for Psycho he made the most famous single decision in film-music history: scoring a black-and-white picture for strings alone, a monochrome orchestra to match the monochrome image, and attacking the shower murder with stabbing, shrieking violin glissandi. Hitchcock had initially wanted the murder to play with no music, only water and knife; he heard Herrmann's cue, reversed himself completely, and raised the composer's fee. He later said, in effect, that a third of Psycho's effect was the music.

Just as characteristic is the score he refused. The Birds has no conventional music at all. Its bird cries and wing beats were built electronically on the mixtur-trautonium, an early electronic instrument, by the German composers Oskar Sala and Remi Gassmann, with Herrmann credited as sound consultant, and the film's most frightening passages are its quietest, the schoolyard filling with crows behind an oblivious Tippi Hedren while a children's song runs out its verses. Hitchcock understood silence as a musical value: the crop-duster sequence in North by Northwest plays for minutes with no score whatever, only wind, distant traffic and an approaching engine, and the absence is what makes the sequence feel so exposed.

The partnership ended badly and instructively. By 1966 Universal wanted contemporary, chart-friendly scores, and Hitchcock, under studio pressure, instructed Herrmann accordingly for the Cold War thriller Torn Curtain. Herrmann wrote what he believed the film needed instead, a brooding orchestral score; Hitchcock arrived at the recording session, heard it, cancelled the sessions and dismissed him, and the two never worked together again. The rejected score is now recorded and admired, the film's replacement music is forgotten, and the episode is cited in every account of the fraught politics between directors, composers and studios. But the decade of collaboration stands: Herrmann's Psycho strings are, note for note, probably the most imitated cue in cinema, quoted, parodied and licensed endlessly, instantly legible to people who have never seen the film.

sections.heading: The Wrong Man, Guilt and Hitchcock's Recurring Themes
sections.body:
Across half a century Hitchcock told, again and again, the story of an ordinary man accused of a crime he did not commit. The lodger suspected of murder in 1927; Richard Hannay hunted across Scotland in The 39 Steps; the saboteur-accused factory worker of Saboteur in 1942; Father Logan in I Confess in 1953, unable to clear himself of murder because the true confession came to him in the confessional; Roger Thornhill in North by Northwest, mistaken for a spy who does not even exist; the flower-seller framed for the necktie murders in Frenzy in 1972. The purest statement is The Wrong Man, from 1956, the closest Hitchcock came to documentary: the true story of Manny Balestrero, a Stork Club bass player played by Henry Fonda, misidentified as an armed robber in Queens in 1953, processed through arrest, arraignment and trial while his wife's mental health collapsed under the strain. Hitchcock opens the film on camera, in silhouette, telling the audience that this story is true, and shoots the machinery of justice, fingerprinting, the cell, the handcuffs, with a dread that is plainly personal.

It was personal. Hitchcock told the story all his life of being sent, as a small boy, to the local police station with a note from his father; the sergeant read it and locked the child in a cell for a few minutes, saying this is what we do to naughty boys. Biographers debate the anecdote's literal truth, but its function is clear: he offered it as the origin of his lifelong fear of police and of arrest, and whatever its accuracy, the fear is stamped on the films. Authority in Hitchcock is never a refuge. The police pursue the innocent efficiently and the guilty rarely; rescue comes from the hero's own wits or from a partner won over one doubt at a time.

Under the wrong-man plot runs a darker current that critics, beginning with the French, learned to call the transference of guilt. Hitchcock's innocents are never quite innocent; accusation attaches to them because something in them answers to it. Strangers on a Train, from 1951, is the theme made architecture: the tennis star Guy wishes his estranged wife gone, the psychopath Bruno murders her unasked, proposing that Guy owes him a murder in exchange, and the film's criss-cross structure keeps insisting that Bruno is Guy's wish walking around in a body. In Shadow of a Doubt the adoring niece shares her uncle's name, his telepathy and, the film hints, his contempt for the complacent world, and destroying him costs her the knowledge that she could. Psycho seats the audience itself in the dock: having spent forty minutes complicit with a thief, viewers are moved to root for a killer sinking a car, and the car's pause halfway into the swamp catches every viewer wishing it under.

Critics have long connected this moral universe to Hitchcock's Catholic formation, its categories of sin, confession and unearned guilt, and he half-accepted the reading. Whatever its source, the theme is what separates his thrillers from their thousand imitations: the suspense machinery runs on the audience's own conscience, and the films are finally about the guilt of the spectator, watching, wishing and enjoying it.

sections.heading: Stars, Blondes and the Director's Treatment of Actresses
sections.body:
Hitchcock's handling of actors is a study in contradictions. He is the source of one of Hollywood's most repeated quips, that actors are cattle, though he insisted he had been misquoted and had only said actors should be treated like cattle; either way the remark advertised his conviction that performance was one element among many, to be designed like a camera move. In practice he worked superbly with stars and made several of them. Cary Grant, across Suspicion, Notorious, To Catch a Thief and North by Northwest, did the most shadowed work of his career for Hitchcock, his charm repeatedly weaponized into ambiguity. James Stewart, across Rope, Rear Window, The Man Who Knew Too Much and Vertigo, was pushed furthest of all: Vertigo turns the era's emblem of decency into an obsessive who remakes a living woman into a dead one, and audiences in 1958, disliking what they saw, made the film a relative failure. Its rehabilitation took decades and ended at the summit: in the British Film Institute's Sight and Sound critics' poll of 2012, Vertigo displaced Citizen Kane as the greatest film ever made.

Then there are the blondes. Hitchcock's casting ran to a repeated feminine type, elegant, cool, self-possessed and blonde, Madeleine Carroll in the 1930s, Ingrid Bergman in the 1940s, Grace Kelly above all in Dial M for Murder, Rear Window and To Catch a Thief, then Kim Novak, Eva Marie Saint, Janet Leigh and Tippi Hedren. He theorized the preference openly: the cool surface, he said, concealed fire, and the concealment was the drama; he disliked actresses whose sexuality was, in his phrase, hung around their necks like jewelry. Critics have read the pattern less kindly, noting how often the films punish these women, strip them of composure, or, in Vertigo's explicit subject, remake them to a man's specification. The films themselves seem intermittently aware of this, Vertigo most of all, which is why it reads today as both symptom and diagnosis.

The record has a genuinely dark chapter. Tippi Hedren, whom Hitchcock discovered in a television commercial and put under personal contract, starred in The Birds in 1963 and Marnie in 1964. For The Birds' climactic attic scene, she was assured mechanical birds would be used, then subjected to five days of live gulls and crows hurled and tethered at her, ending in collapse and a week ordered off work by a physician. In interviews and in her 2016 memoir, Hedren stated that Hitchcock sexually propositioned and assaulted her, isolated her on set, and, when she refused him and asked out of her contract, told her he would ruin her career, then kept her under contract and unavailable for other work. Hitchcock died decades before the account was fully published; some colleagues have disputed details, and Hedren has stood by it. Most Hitchcock scholarship now holds the two things in the same hand: the films' greatness is real, and so, on the evidence, was serious abuse of power over a dependent employee.

For working actors, his sets were nonetheless famously calm, even boring: the film was already made on paper, he said, and shooting was transcription. Performers who thrived under him, Stewart, Grant, Kelly, Leigh, described precise, minimal direction, faith in casting, and a director who knew exactly which sixty seconds of their work the film would use.

sections.heading: The Great 1950s Run: Rear Window, Vertigo and North by Northwest
sections.body:
No director has had a decade like Hitchcock's 1950s. Free of Selznick, commanding his own unit, and working with collaborators at their peak, the cinematographer Robert Burks, the editor George Tomasini, the composer Bernard Herrmann and the costume designer Edith Head, he released, in sequence, Strangers on a Train in 1951, Dial M for Murder and Rear Window in 1954, To Catch a Thief in 1955, The Trouble with Harry the same year, the remake of The Man Who Knew Too Much in 1956, The Wrong Man in 1956, Vertigo in 1958 and North by Northwest in 1959, then opened the next decade with Psycho in 1960. At the same time he was hosting Alfred Hitchcock Presents on television, whose weekly ten-minute masterclasses in economy fed directly into Psycho's lean production. Any three of those films would anchor a career; together they are the core curriculum of the thriller.

Rear Window is the formal masterpiece, an entire feature staged across a single Greenwich Village courtyard built on a Paramount soundstage, said to be among the largest indoor sets yet constructed there, with working apartments, rain effects and lighting for day and night. James Stewart's photographer, leg in a cast, watches his neighbors through the heat wave, assembling from fragments the conviction that the salesman opposite has murdered his wife. Every neighbor's window is a variation on marriage, the newlyweds, the songwriter, Miss Lonelyhearts, so the suspense plot doubles as an essay on the hero's own fear of commitment to Grace Kelly's Lisa, who proves her worth to him, pointedly, only when she crosses the courtyard and enters the dangerous frame he has been watching like a screen. The film is Hitchcock's cleanest statement about spectatorship: the audience cannot condemn the voyeur without condemning itself.

Vertigo, adapted from the French novel D'entre les morts, is the confession. A detective, retired by his acrophobia, is hired to follow a friend's wife, saves her from drowning, loves her, loses her to a fall his vertigo prevents him from stopping, and then finds a shopgirl who resembles her and remakes the girl, clothes, hair, walk, into the dead woman, unaware he is reconstructing a fraud in which he was the audience. Shot in San Francisco in saturated Technicolor, scored by Herrmann in unresolved spirals, it moves at the pace of obsession rather than suspense, and it failed commercially in 1958 precisely because it is not the film its poster promised. Its slow rise to the top of the 2012 Sight and Sound poll tracked a change in what viewers wanted from Hitchcock: not the machine, but the machinist's psyche.

North by Northwest is the machine at maximum polish, written by Ernest Lehman, who said he set out to make the Hitchcock picture to end all Hitchcock pictures. Cary Grant's Madison Avenue adman is mistaken for a nonexistent agent, framed for a murder at the United Nations, hunted across the country to a finale on Mount Rushmore, and ambushed by a crop-dusting plane in a flat, empty Indiana cornfield, a sequence Hitchcock designed as a deliberate inversion of the genre's dark-alley clichés: total exposure, broad daylight, nowhere to hide and no music. Its blend of glamour, comedy, chase structure and set-piece engineering is the direct template for the James Bond series that began three years later, and through Bond, for the modern action blockbuster generally.

sections.heading: Psycho, The Birds and the Late Career
sections.body:
Psycho began as a dare Hitchcock made to himself. Paramount disliked the material, a pulp novel by Robert Bloch inspired by the Wisconsin killer Ed Gein, and refused normal financing, so Hitchcock financed it personally, deferred his fee for sixty percent of the picture, shot in black and white on a budget of about eight hundred thousand dollars, and used the fast television crew from Alfred Hitchcock Presents. Every constraint became an aesthetic. The cheap monochrome matched the story's shabby motels and hard cash; the small crew kept the secret; and the secrecy became the marketing, with theaters contractually barred from admitting anyone after the picture started, a genuinely new exhibition practice that trained audiences to arrive on time and guard endings. The film returned its cost many times over, became the most profitable film of Hitchcock's career, and made its director, at sixty, the idol of a new young audience. It also drew a line across film history: the modern horror film, with its contemporary settings, its violated bathrooms and its killers shaped by psychology rather than cobwebs, starts here, and the slasher cycle of the late 1970s, Halloween explicitly included, is its direct descendant. Anthony Perkins's Norman Bates, boyish, stammering and sympathetic until the last reel, replaced the monster with the boy next door.

The Birds, in 1963, was the last of his films built on a massive technical gamble. From a Daphne du Maurier story, it strands a Northern California coastal town, Bodega Bay, under inexplicable mass bird attacks, refuses to the end any explanation, and closes without the words The End, on an unresolved image of survivors driving slowly through a landscape carpeted with waiting birds. The film required years of preparation, hundreds of trick shots combining trained birds, mechanical birds and the sodium-vapor matte process borrowed from Disney, and, as the previous sections describe, an electronic soundscape in place of a score and a production ordeal for its star, Tippi Hedren, that has permanently marked its reputation. As pure apocalyptic cinema, an ordinary world withdrawing its cooperation without motive, it has never been surpassed in his work, and its refusal of explanation was a bigger risk than any effect in it.

The last act was quieter. Marnie, in 1964, a psychosexual case study starring Hedren and Sean Connery, was dismissed at the time and has been substantially revalued since. The Cold War pictures Torn Curtain, in 1966, and Topaz, in 1969, were troubled productions and are the weakest of his sound films. Frenzy, made in London in 1972, was a genuine late return of force, his first film under the new ratings freedom, and its necktie-murder sequence, and the celebrated shot in which the camera retreats backward down a staircase and out into street noise while a murder proceeds unseen upstairs, showed the old command intact and newly frank. His final film, Family Plot, a kidnapping comedy-thriller, appeared in 1976. He was preparing another project, The Short Night, when his health failed; he was knighted at the end of 1979, honorarily, having been an American citizen since 1955, and died at home in Bel Air on April 29, 1980, at the age of eighty.

sections.heading: Hitchcock's Legacy: How the Thriller Learned Its Grammar
sections.body:
Hitchcock's afterlife began, oddly, in Paris. In the 1950s the young critics of Cahiers du Cinema, Francois Truffaut, Claude Chabrol, Eric Rohmer and Jean-Luc Godard among them, seized on Hitchcock as the test case for what became the auteur theory: the claim that a director working inside the commercial studio system could be the true author of his films, with a personal style and moral universe as coherent as a novelist's. Chabrol and Rohmer published the first serious book on him in 1957; Truffaut's week of recorded interviews in 1962, published in 1966 as Hitchcock/Truffaut, remains probably the most influential book of film craft ever printed, the volume through which generations of filmmakers absorbed the bomb theory, the MacGuffin and the primacy of the shot. The American critical establishment, which had long filed Hitchcock under skilled entertainer, largely came around; the Sight and Sound poll that crowned Vertigo in 2012 completed a fifty-year revaluation.

His practical influence is so pervasive it is easiest to see in lists. The suspense grammar, audience knowledge running ahead of character knowledge, is the operating system of the modern thriller, from heist films to horror. The dolly zoom he built for Vertigo is a stock expressive tool. The shower scene's rapid montage is the ancestor of modern action cutting, and Psycho's mid-film murder of its star licensed every storyteller since to kill a protagonist for structural shock. The no-late-admission policy pioneered spoiler culture and event exhibition. The chase-picture template of North by Northwest was, by the Bond producers' own acknowledgment, foundational to that series and through it to the action blockbuster. Television anthology horror, from The Twilight Zone onward, worked ground Alfred Hitchcock Presents had cleared. Even film theory owes him: Laura Mulvey's 1975 essay on the male gaze, a founding text of feminist film criticism, takes Rear Window and Vertigo as its central exhibits, and the fact that his films can sustain both celebration and indictment is itself a measure of their density.

Individual careers descend from him openly. Brian De Palma built half a filmography, Sisters, Obsession, Dressed to Kill, Body Double, on explicit Hitchcock variations. Steven Spielberg's Jaws is the bomb theory with a fin, its shark withheld like the bomb under the table; Spielberg has called Hitchcock a permanent reference. Martin Scorsese, David Fincher, Jonathan Demme, whose The Silence of the Lambs climaxes on pure Hitchcockian cross-cut misdirection, Park Chan-wook, M. Night Shyamalan and Jordan Peele have all worked and acknowledged his vocabulary; Gus Van Sant went as far as a shot-for-shot Psycho remake in 1998, an experiment whose flatness proved, better than any essay, that the films are not their screenplays but their execution.

The critical reckoning is genuinely double-sided now: the Hedren allegations and the films' patterns with women are part of any honest account, taught alongside the technique rather than instead of it. What is not in dispute is the scale of the technical bequest. Hitchcock did more than anyone to demonstrate that popular cinema could be an exact art, that fear and suspense are built from shot size, cutting rhythm, sound and withheld information, and that the audience's mind is the screen on which the real film plays. Every thriller made since negotiates with that demonstration, whether its maker knows the source or not.

guides.title: Orson Welles and Citizen Kane
guides.summary: The making, meaning and afterlife of Citizen Kane, and the career of the director who made it at twenty-five. It covers Welles's theatre and radio apprenticeship, the unprecedented RKO contract, the authorship dispute, the film's deep-focus photography and sound design, the campaign to suppress it, and the long argument over whether it is really the greatest film ever made.

sections.heading: Why One Film From 1941 Still Sets the Terms
sections.body:
For five consecutive decades, from 1962 to 2002, the critics' poll conducted every ten years by the British magazine Sight and Sound named Citizen Kane the greatest film ever made. No other work has held that position for so long, and few works in any medium have been so consistently used as a benchmark. When the poll finally moved on — to Vertigo in 2012 and to Chantal Akerman's Jeanne Dielman in 2022 — the news was reported as though a monarch had died, which is itself a measure of how thoroughly the film had become the fixed point against which everything else was placed.

The reputation rests on an unusual combination. Citizen Kane was made by a twenty-five-year-old with no previous experience of directing a feature film, working under a contract that gave him more freedom than any newcomer had ever received from a Hollywood studio, on a subject that risked the enmity of the most powerful publisher in the United States. It failed commercially on release, won a single Academy Award out of nine nominations, and was substantially unavailable for a decade. Its canonisation came later and from outside the American industry that produced it.

What makes the film important technically is not that it invented its techniques. Deep-focus photography, low-angle shots showing ceilings, elaborate sound bridges, non-linear narration and flashbacks told by multiple unreliable witnesses all existed before 1941, in Hollywood and in European and Japanese cinema. What Kane did was assemble them into a single self-conscious demonstration, executed with such confidence and in such density that it functioned as a catalogue of possibilities. Directors and cinematographers who saw it understood that the conventional grammar of studio filmmaking was a choice rather than a necessity. The film's real influence lies in that permission.

Its subject matter is equally durable. The film examines a man who acquires wealth, newspapers, political ambition, two wives and an enormous private palace, and dies alone having failed to obtain the one thing he wanted. It is about the impossibility of summing up a life, and it is structured to demonstrate that impossibility: five witnesses give five partial and contradictory accounts, a reporter fails to find the answer he was sent for, and the audience is shown a solution the characters never learn. That the solution — a burning sled — is deliberately trivial is the point, and it was recognised as such at the time. The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges, reviewing the film in 1941, called it a labyrinth with no centre, and meant it as both praise and criticism.

Understanding Citizen Kane properly means understanding four separate things: the theatrical and radio apprenticeship that produced its methods, the industrial circumstances that made it possible, the craft decisions that make it look and sound the way it does, and the long argument about who deserves credit for it.

sections.heading: Welles Before Hollywood: The Theatre Years
sections.body:
George Orson Welles was born in Kenosha, Wisconsin, on 6 May 1915, into a comfortable and unstable household. His mother, a pianist and suffragist, died when he was nine; his father, an inventor and businessman, died when he was fifteen. He was raised largely by a family friend, Dr Maurice Bernstein, and was educated at the Todd Seminary for Boys in Woodstock, Illinois, where a sympathetic headmaster let him stage plays with essentially unlimited licence. He was treated as a prodigy from early childhood and had, by his own later account, entirely absorbed the assumption.

At sixteen he travelled to Ireland and talked his way onto the stage of Dublin's Gate Theatre by claiming to be an established Broadway star, an audacity that worked well enough to get him leading roles. He returned to the United States, co-edited an annotated Shakespeare series for schools, and by 1934 was working in New York. In 1936, aged twenty-one, he directed for the Negro Theatre Unit of the Federal Theatre Project — the New Deal programme that employed out-of-work theatre people — a production of Macbeth with an all-Black cast, relocated from Scotland to a Haiti-like Caribbean court and using Haitian drummers and Vodou imagery. Known ever since as the Voodoo Macbeth, it played to enormous crowds at the Lafayette Theatre in Harlem and made him nationally visible.

In 1937 he staged Marc Blitzstein's pro-union musical The Cradle Will Rock, which the government shut down four days before opening amid congressional pressure over the Federal Theatre Project's politics. Welles and his producing partner John Houseman marched the audience twenty blocks to another theatre and performed it with the composer at an upright piano and the cast singing from their seats in the auditorium, since union rules forbade them from appearing on stage. The story became legend, and it is a fair illustration of a lifelong pattern: obstacles converted into showmanship.

Welles and Houseman then founded the Mercury Theatre, whose first production, later in 1937, was Julius Caesar staged in modern dress with the conspirators in fascist uniforms and Caesar as a Mussolini figure, on a bare brick stage lit by vertical shafts of light modelled on the Nuremberg rallies. It ran for 157 performances. The company assembled there — Joseph Cotten, Everett Sloane, Agnes Moorehead, Ray Collins, George Coulouris, Paul Stewart — is the same company that would appear in Citizen Kane, and this matters more than it might appear. Welles arrived in Hollywood with a trained ensemble accustomed to his working methods, none of whom carried a screen persona the audience already knew, which is a large part of why the characters in Kane seem to be people rather than stars.

sections.heading: Radio, and the Night of the Martians
sections.body:
Welles's other apprenticeship was in radio, and it shaped Citizen Kane at least as much as the theatre did. Through the mid-1930s he worked constantly as a radio actor, most famously as the voice of the crime-fighting Lamont Cranston in The Shadow, and by 1938 CBS had given the Mercury company its own series, The Mercury Theatre on the Air, adapting novels and plays for a weekly hour.

Radio drama taught lessons that transfer directly to cinema. Because the listener cannot see, space must be conveyed through sound alone: the reverberation of a large hall, the deadness of a small room, the way a voice changes as a speaker moves away from the microphone. Welles became expert at building acoustic environments, at using overlapping dialogue so that conversations sound like real simultaneous speech rather than tidy alternation, and at the sound bridge that carries a listener from one scene to another without narration. He also became expert at the fake documentary register — the authoritative newsreader's cadence, the bulletin, the on-the-spot report.

On the evening of 30 October 1938 the Mercury broadcast an adaptation of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds, restructured by Howard Koch as a sequence of interrupted dance-band music and increasingly alarming news bulletins describing a Martian landing at Grover's Mill, New Jersey. The programme carried announcements identifying it as fiction, but listeners tuning in late heard what sounded exactly like breaking news in a year when breaking news from Europe was genuinely alarming.

The extent of the resulting panic is a case where the popular story outruns the evidence, and honesty requires saying so. Newspapers the next day reported mass hysteria, and the incident entered folklore as proof of radio's hypnotic power. Later scholarship, notably by Jefferson Pooley and Michael Socolow, has argued that the audience was small — the programme was scheduled opposite the far more popular Chase and Sanborn Hour — and that press coverage was amplified by a newspaper industry with a commercial motive to discredit radio as an advertising rival. Some listeners were undoubtedly frightened and some telephoned police; a nationwide stampede is not well supported. What is beyond dispute is the effect on Welles's career: at twenty-three he was on the cover of Time, and Hollywood came calling.

The techniques of that broadcast reappear directly in Citizen Kane. The News on the March newsreel that opens the film is the visual equivalent of the fake bulletin, complete with a portentous narrator, and the film's dialogue overlaps and interrupts in a way that was startling to audiences accustomed to the clean alternation of studio sound recording. Welles never stopped being a radio man; he narrated and performed on the air for the rest of his life.

sections.heading: The Contract That Made It Possible
sections.body:
In 1939 RKO Radio Pictures was in trouble. It was the smallest and least stable of the five major Hollywood studios, had emerged from receivership only a year earlier, and had a new president, George J. Schaefer, who believed the way back was prestige pictures made by exceptional talent. Schaefer pursued Welles aggressively, and the contract signed in July 1939 became legendary in the industry for how much it conceded.

The terms are worth stating precisely, because the film that resulted is unimaginable without them. Welles was contracted for two pictures, on which he would act as producer, director, writer and star as he chose. He had the right to develop his own material and to shoot without studio supervision on set. Most extraordinarily, he had final cut: the studio could not re-edit the finished film. He was not permitted to exceed an agreed budget, and RKO retained approval of the story, so the freedom was not unlimited, but for a twenty-four-year-old who had never made a feature it was unprecedented and was recognised as such.

The reaction in Hollywood was hostile. Established directors and producers regarded the deal as an insult, and the press mocked the arrangement — Welles's beard, his lack of film experience and his self-assurance were all reliable copy. He did not help himself by describing a film studio, on first seeing one, as the biggest electric train set a boy ever had. That line followed him for the rest of his life, usually quoted by people arguing that he was a dilettante.

Welles spent months learning. He watched films repeatedly in the RKO screening room with the studio's staff to explain technique, above all John Ford's Stagecoach, which he later claimed to have run something like forty times. He developed and abandoned two projects first: an adaptation of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, to be shot almost entirely from the protagonist's point of view with the camera as his eyes, which was budgeted at a figure RKO would not accept; and a thriller called The Smiler with a Knife. The failure of Heart of Darkness matters, because the elaborate preparation Welles did for it — subjective camera, extensive storyboarding, the technical problems of lenses and lighting — was effectively a paid education in filmmaking that he then applied to Kane.

The budget finally set for the picture that became Citizen Kane was modest for a prestige production. Figures cited vary slightly between sources, but the final negative cost is generally given as roughly 840,000 dollars, against an original budget in the region of 700,000. Shooting proceeded from late June 1940, initially disguised on the schedule as camera tests so that Welles could begin before formal approval, and continued into October. The cast was almost entirely the Mercury company making their film debuts, which kept salaries low and gave Welles a company that already trusted him.

sections.heading: Who Wrote It: The Mankiewicz Question
sections.body:
The screenplay was begun by Herman J. Mankiewicz, a witty, alcoholic, formidably well-connected screenwriter who had been a New York theatre critic and a Hollywood fixture since the 1920s, and who had known William Randolph Hearst socially, having been a guest at his California estate. In early 1940 Mankiewicz was sent, with a broken leg and under the supervision of John Houseman, to a ranch at Victorville in the Mojave Desert, partly to work and partly to keep him away from drink. There he produced a very long first draft, originally titled American.

Welles then worked on the material extensively, cutting it down, restructuring it and rewriting dialogue, in a process that continued through pre-production and into shooting. The final screen credit read Herman J. Mankiewicz and Orson Welles, and the two shared the film's only Academy Award, for Best Original Screenplay. Welles reportedly attempted at one stage to take sole credit, and the Screen Writers Guild intervened; accounts of this episode differ and depend on whose memoir one reads.

The dispute became public and bitter in 1971, when the critic Pauline Kael published a long two-part essay in The New Yorker, later issued as Raising Kane, arguing that Mankiewicz was essentially the sole author and that Welles's reputation rested on appropriating another man's work. The essay was superbly written, hugely influential, and substantially wrong in its methods: Kael did not consult the surviving script drafts, relied heavily on interested witnesses, and later research established that at least one of her research assistants' findings had been used without acknowledgement.

The rebuttals came quickly. Peter Bogdanovich published a defence in Esquire in 1972, drawing on Welles's own account. More decisively, the film scholar Robert L. Carringer examined the seven successive script drafts held in the RKO and Mercury archives and published The Making of Citizen Kane in 1985, demonstrating a substantial and traceable Welles contribution — particularly to the structure, to the compression of the narrative and to a great deal of the dialogue in the final draft — while confirming that the foundational architecture, the Hearst material and many of the best lines were Mankiewicz's.

The honest modern verdict is that both men have a genuine claim and that the argument has often been a proxy for something else: hostility to the auteur theory, which held the director to be a film's author, or defence of the undervalued screenwriter. David Fincher's 2020 film Mank revived the Kael version for a new audience, which irritated many Welles scholars. What is not in dispute is that the direction, the visual design, the sound and the performances are Welles's, and that a screenplay is not a film.

sections.heading: Hearst, Marion Davies and the Real-World Models
sections.body:
Charles Foster Kane is not William Randolph Hearst, but the resemblance is close enough that everyone recognised it immediately, and the differences matter as much as the similarities.

Hearst, born in 1863, inherited a mining fortune and used it to buy the San Francisco Examiner, then the New York Morning Journal, building the largest newspaper chain in the United States and pioneering the sensationalist style known as yellow journalism. He agitated for war with Spain in 1898. He served two terms in Congress, ran unsuccessfully for Mayor of New York and for Governor, and harboured presidential ambitions that never materialised. He built an extravagant hilltop estate at San Simeon in California, filled with art bought by the shipload. He lived openly for decades with the actress Marion Davies while remaining married. All of this is transposed to Kane, whose Xanadu is San Simeon and whose political career collapses in a sex scandal.

The film also borrows from other men. Samuel Insull, the Chicago utilities magnate, built an opera house partly to provide a venue for a singer; Harold McCormick of the International Harvester fortune spent lavishly promoting the operatic career of his wife Ganna Walska, whose talent was widely considered insufficient. Kane's separation from his parents and his upbringing by a bank draws on no single model. Mankiewicz reportedly insisted the character was a composite, which was both true and legally convenient.

The most serious unfairness is to Marion Davies. Susan Alexander in the film is a talentless singer, humiliated by a career her husband forces upon her, who ends as an alcoholic in a nightclub. Davies was in reality a gifted comic actress, well liked in Hollywood, whose career in light comedy was genuinely successful and was arguably harmed rather than helped by Hearst's insistence on casting her in heavy historical dramas. She was also loyal to Hearst to the end, reportedly offering him her own money during his financial difficulties in the 1930s. Welles came to regret the portrayal and said so publicly in later years, writing a foreword to a book about Davies in which he acknowledged the injustice.

The persistent rumour that Rosebud was Hearst's private nickname for an intimate part of Davies's anatomy is repeated constantly and cannot be verified; it appears to originate in Hollywood gossip and was propagated by Kael. If true, it would explain the ferocity of Hearst's response better than the general portrait does. Whether or not it is true, Hearst's newspapers behaved as though something intolerably personal had been touched.

It is worth adding that the film is not a simple attack. Kane is given real charm, real courage in his early crusading years, and a genuinely moving loneliness; the Declaration of Principles he writes as a young publisher is sincere when he writes it, and its later betrayal is presented as a tragedy rather than a fraud. Several critics have argued that the portrait is more sympathetic than Hearst deserved, and Welles maintained that he was interested in the shape of a life rather than in journalism or in any particular man.

sections.heading: The Story and Its Structure
sections.body:
The film opens on a chain-link fence and a No Trespassing sign, and the camera does exactly what the sign forbids, climbing a series of dissolves up through the grounds of a decaying estate to a single lit window. Inside, an old man drops a glass snow globe, whispers a word, and dies. The word is Rosebud.

There follows News on the March, a nine-minute pastiche newsreel that summarises the entire life of Charles Foster Kane in the confident, empty rhetoric of period journalism: the fortune, the newspapers, the two marriages, the failed run for Governor, the unfinished palace called Xanadu, the lonely decline. This is a structurally radical move, because it gives away the whole plot in the first ten minutes. Nothing that follows is suspenseful in the ordinary sense. Having disposed of what happened, the film can spend two hours on the only question that remains, which is what any of it meant.

The newsreel ends in a projection room where its editor, dissatisfied, sends a reporter named Thompson to find out what Rosebud means. Thompson's face is never clearly seen, and he has no character; he is a device for gathering testimony. He consults five sources. The written memoir of Walter Parks Thatcher, the banker who took Kane from his parents as a child, covers the boyhood and the acquisition of the newspaper. Bernstein, the loyal business manager, covers the idealistic early years. Jedediah Leland, the friend Kane eventually betrays, covers the first marriage and the political collapse, and is the film's moral witness. Susan Alexander, the second wife, covers the opera disaster and the misery of Xanadu. Raymond, the butler, covers the last years.

The accounts overlap, contradict one another in detail and in tone, and are shaped by each narrator's interests. This structure — a life reconstructed through incompatible testimony — was not new in literature, but it was startling in a 1941 studio film. It has an important consequence: the audience never receives an authoritative account. Even the chronology is fractured, since scenes return to periods already covered from a new angle.

Thompson gives up, saying that no single word explains a man's life, and that Rosebud is probably just a piece of a jigsaw puzzle. Then, in a final sequence he does not witness, workmen clearing the accumulated junk of Xanadu throw a child's sled into a furnace, and the camera moves close enough to read the trade name burning off it: Rosebud. It is the sled Kane was playing with in the snow on the day he was taken from his mother.

The solution is deliberately unsatisfying, and this is not a flaw. Welles himself called Rosebud rather dollar-book Freud. The point is that a life cannot be resolved by an object, that the audience has been given a fact the characters could not find, and that possessing the fact explains nothing. The word functions as a machine for organising the film rather than as an answer.

sections.heading: Gregg Toland and the Look of Deep Focus
sections.body:
Gregg Toland was the most respected cinematographer in Hollywood, had just won an Academy Award for Wuthering Heights, and could work wherever he liked. He approached Welles and asked to shoot the film, saying he wanted to work with someone who did not know the rules. Welles later said that Toland spent the production quietly teaching him cinematography while allowing him to believe he was inventing it, and in gratitude gave Toland a title card on the same frame as his own director credit, an honour essentially without precedent.

The film's signature look is deep focus: foreground, middle ground and background all held in sharp focus simultaneously, so that action can be staged in depth rather than assembled by cutting. Achieving it required aggressive technical measures, because depth of field increases as the lens aperture narrows and as focal length shortens, and both changes cost light. Toland used wide-angle lenses, notably 24 millimetre and in places 18 millimetre, stopped down to small apertures. He used the newly available Eastman Super XX film stock, roughly twice as fast as previous stocks. He used lenses treated with an anti-reflective coating developed at Bausch and Lomb, marketed as Vard Opticoat, which reduced internal flare and gained useful contrast. And he lit with high-intensity arc lamps at levels that were uncomfortable for the actors.

The effect is not merely technical showmanship, because deep focus changes what a shot means. When everything is sharp, the viewer's eye must choose where to look, and the director can hold two dramatic actions in tension without cutting between them. The most quoted example occurs early: young Charles is seen through a window, playing in the snow, small and bright at the centre of the frame, while in the foreground of the same shot his mother signs the papers that will send him away. The composition states the situation entirely — the child is visible, distant, and unconsulted — without a line of dialogue about it. Later, Susan's attempted suicide is shown with a glass, a spoon and a medicine bottle looming in the foreground while she lies in bed and Kane breaks in through a door at the back of the shot.

The other pronounced choice is the low camera angle. Welles wanted to see ceilings, which conventional sets did not have because the lighting rigs hung above. The production built sets with practical ceilings made of stretched muslin, which the microphones could shoot through, and dug holes in the stage floor so the camera could be placed below floor level. The low angles make Kane monumental in his powerful years and make the rooms of Xanadu oppressive. Some critics have noted honestly that deep focus in Kane is sometimes achieved by optical printing and multiple exposures rather than by a single in-camera take, which does not diminish the effect but does complicate the legend.

sections.heading: Sound: Lightning Mixes, Overlaps and Herrmann's Score
sections.body:
Because Welles came from radio, the soundtrack of Citizen Kane is designed with a deliberateness rare in the period, and much of what feels modern about the film is audible rather than visible.

The most distinctive device is what the Mercury company called the lightning mix: a cut in which a line of dialogue begun in one scene is completed in another, often years later, so that the sound carries the audience across time without a dissolve or a title. The celebrated instance has Thatcher wishing the boy a Merry Christmas in the snow, and the same voice completing the sentence with a happy New Year over a shot of Kane as a young man about fifteen years later. Another has a political speaker introducing Kane, the sentence finishing in a different voice in a different hall. A third has Susan's singing teacher's exasperated exercise continuing across a montage that compresses her entire disastrous opera career, ending with a light bulb dimming and a lone slow handclap.

Dialogue overlaps constantly. Characters interrupt, talk across one another and complete each other's sentences, which had been done before but rarely so systematically. Achieving it required rehearsal and careful microphone placement, since the standard studio practice of clean alternating lines existed partly because overlapping speech is difficult to record and impossible to re-edit freely.

Acoustic space is used as characterisation. Conversations in the vast hall at Xanadu are recorded with heavy reverberation and staged at absurd distances, so that Kane and Susan shout tinny sentences at each other across a room the size of a cathedral, the sound itself conveying the emptiness of the marriage. The newsreel is given the flat, slightly degraded sound of genuine period newsreels, with hiss and horn-speaker tone, and the negative was deliberately scratched and dust was blown at the print to age it.

The score is by Bernard Herrmann, who had worked with Welles in radio and for whom this was a first film score. Herrmann later wrote for Hitchcock, including Vertigo and Psycho, and became one of the medium's major composers. His work here avoids the continuous lush underscore then standard, using instead short cellular motifs — a brooding five-note figure for power, a lighter one for Rosebud — that recur transformed. He was given an unusually long twelve weeks and wrote music in advance for several sequences, so that image was cut to music rather than the reverse. He also composed a convincing pastiche of a French-oriental opera, Salammbô, deliberately pitched so that the aria sits cruelly above the range of a soprano of Susan's limited ability, so the audience hears her failing rather than being told about it.

sections.heading: Editing, Montage and the Breakfast Table
sections.body:
The film was edited by Robert Wise, then a young RKO staff editor who would later direct The Day the Earth Stood Still, West Side Story and The Sound of Music, assisted by Mark Robson, who also became a director. Their contribution is frequently underrated in accounts that treat the film as a solitary act of genius.

The best-known passage is the breakfast table sequence, which portrays the disintegration of Kane's first marriage in roughly two minutes. It begins with the newlyweds affectionate and close, sharing one end of a table, and proceeds through a series of short exchanges separated by rapid whip pans — a violent horizontal swish of the camera that blurs the image and disguises the cut. Each fragment jumps forward in time by an unstated interval. The dialogue cools from flirtation to complaint to accusation. The costumes become more formal, the lighting harder, the table longer. The final beat has the couple in silence at opposite ends of a vast table, she reading a rival newspaper. Nothing is explained; the audience simply watches nine years happen. The device is a compressed version of the montage sequence common in 1930s cinema, but used for interior emotional change rather than for the usual purpose of showing a career taking off or a season passing.

Elsewhere the cutting is comparatively slow, because deep-focus staging lets scenes play in long takes with the actors moving in depth. This alternation between passages of extreme compression and passages of extended unbroken time is a structural rhythm, and it is one of the things later filmmakers took from the picture. The film also uses dissolves as a mode of thought rather than as mere transitions — the opening ascent to Xanadu is a chain of dissolves in which the lit window remains in the same position in each frame, so that the estate changes around a fixed point of attention.

Two other technical elements deserve mention. The special effects, supervised by Vernon L. Walker, are extensive and largely invisible: many of the grandest views of Xanadu are matte paintings, and a good deal of apparent depth is achieved through optical printing that combines separately shot foreground and background elements. The makeup by Maurice Seiderman, who was not then a senior member of the department, ages a cast of young actors across half a century, using built-up prosthetic pieces, contact lenses to dull the eyes and thinned hairlines. Welles is convincing at twenty-five playing a man of seventy, and the ageing is one of the reasons audiences accept a company of unknown stage actors as figures of national consequence. Seiderman received no screen credit for the work, an omission that irritated Welles, who reportedly held up the film's completion until a card was added.

sections.heading: The Campaign to Bury the Film
sections.body:
Word of the film's subject reached the Hearst organisation before it was finished, apparently through the gossip columnist Louella Parsons, who worked for Hearst and who was shown the picture and reacted with fury. What followed was one of the most determined attempts to suppress an American film ever mounted, and it very nearly succeeded.

Hearst's newspapers, which reached a large fraction of the American reading public, refused all advertising for the film and for a period refused to mention RKO productions at all. Reporters and columnists in the chain attacked Welles personally, and there were attempts to raise questions about his politics at a moment when accusations of communist sympathy carried professional danger. Pressure was applied to theatre chains not to book the picture.

The most striking episode is the offer to destroy it. Louis B. Mayer of MGM, acting on behalf of a group of studio heads anxious about the industry's relationship with the press, reportedly offered RKO the sum of 805,000 dollars — roughly the film's negative cost — on condition that the negative be burned. Schaefer refused. The refusal is a genuine act of courage in an industry not known for it, and Schaefer's career suffered for it; he left RKO in 1942.

The suppression was partially effective in a way that mattered commercially. The major theatre circuits, several of which were owned by other studios, were reluctant to book the film, and it opened on 1 May 1941 at the RKO Palace in New York in a limited release, playing in relatively few cinemas. Reviews were largely excellent — the New York Times, Variety and the trade press recognised it as extraordinary — but a prestige picture that cannot get into theatres cannot recover its cost. Citizen Kane lost money on first release, with the loss usually put at around 150,000 dollars, and RKO withdrew it into the vaults.

There is a persistent irony worth noting. Hearst's campaign is the main reason the film failed commercially, and also a large part of the reason it became famous. The story of the suppressed masterpiece attached itself to the picture permanently and guaranteed that it would be sought out later. There is no evidence Hearst ever saw the film. He lived until 1951, and his own reputation was affected by a portrait he had tried to prevent.

The film's rehabilitation began after the war and largely in Europe. It was reissued in the United States in 1956, and the arrival of television and repertory screening put it in front of audiences who had never had the chance to see it. French critics writing for Cahiers du cinéma, then constructing the argument that a film's director is its author, treated Kane as the founding demonstration of their case, and the reputation flowed back across the Atlantic from there.

sections.heading: Awards, Reception and the Long Climb to Canonisation
sections.body:
At the Academy Awards in February 1942 the film received nine nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actor for Welles, and Best Cinematography for Toland. It won one: Best Original Screenplay, shared by Mankiewicz and Welles. Contemporary reports say that the mention of the film's name at the ceremony drew audible booing from sections of the audience, though the reliability of such accounts is imperfect. Best Picture went to John Ford's How Green Was My Valley, a decision now routinely cited as evidence that award voting reflects industry politics as much as merit, though Ford's film has its own substantial defenders.

Critical opinion at the time was not unanimous. Several reviewers found the technique showy and the central character cold, and the complaint that the film is an exercise in virtuosity around an emotional void has never entirely gone away. Borges, in a 1941 review, praised its intelligence while calling it a labyrinth with no centre and predicting that it would be admired rather than loved.

The rise to canonical status can be dated fairly precisely. In 1952 the film placed well down the first Sight and Sound critics' poll, which was topped by Bicycle Thieves. In 1958 a poll of critics at the Brussels World's Fair placed it high. In the 1962 Sight and Sound poll it reached first place, and it stayed there in 1972, 1982, 1992 and 2002 — five consecutive decennial polls, a run no other film has matched. The American Film Institute placed it first in its 1998 list of the hundred greatest American films and again in the 2007 revision. It was among the first twenty-five films selected for the United States National Film Registry in 1989.

The 2012 poll displaced it, with Hitchcock's Vertigo taking first place by a margin of thirty-four votes, and in 2022 the greatly expanded poll placed Jeanne Dielman first, Vertigo second and Kane third. The shift reflects a widened and more international body of voters, a reaction against a choice that had come to feel automatic, and a genuine broadening of what critics value. None of this constitutes a discovery that the film is bad. A work that occupies the top position for fifty years and then settles into the top three has not been debunked.

A further point about reputation is worth making plainly. Being called the greatest film ever made is a poor way to encounter anything, because it sets an expectation of overwhelming impact that a seventy-year-old black-and-white picture in an unfamiliar idiom will rarely deliver on a first viewing. Kane rewards a second and third viewing far more than a first, because much of what it does — the layering of testimony, the staging in depth, the aural jokes — is designed to be noticed rather than felt.

sections.heading: The Rest of a Career: Ambersons to Exile
sections.body:
Welles was twenty-six when Citizen Kane was released and lived another forty-four years, during which he completed roughly a dozen further features and left a larger number unfinished. The shape of that career is the second half of the story, and it is frequently told as pure tragedy, which is not quite right.

His second RKO film, The Magnificent Ambersons, adapted from Booth Tarkington's novel about a wealthy family displaced by the automobile age, was in some respects more ambitious than Kane. While Welles was in Brazil filming a government-sponsored documentary project called It's All True, the studio previewed Ambersons to a poor response, cut it from roughly 132 minutes to 88, shot a new happy ending with another director, and destroyed the excised footage. Welles had lost the final-cut protection when the terms of his arrangement changed. The mutilated film remains extraordinary; the lost hour is the most lamented missing footage in American cinema, and repeated searches have failed to find it.

What followed was a career of remarkable pictures made under impossible conditions. The Lady from Shanghai in 1947 contains the hall-of-mirrors shootout that has been imitated ever since. Macbeth in 1948 was shot in twenty-three days on borrowed Western sets. Othello, assembled over three years across Morocco and Italy as funds appeared and vanished, won the top prize at Cannes in 1952; a famous scene was staged in a Turkish bath because the costumes had not arrived. Touch of Evil in 1958 opens with a continuous crane shot of more than three minutes following a car with a bomb in its boot, and was again re-cut by the studio, prompting a fifty-eight-page memo from Welles that was used in 1998 as the basis for a restoration. Chimes at Midnight in 1966, assembling Shakespeare's Falstaff from several plays, is regarded by many critics, and was regarded by Welles, as his best work. F for Fake in 1973 is an essay film about forgery and authorship that anticipates a whole later genre.

He financed much of this by acting, often in poor films, and by voicing commercials, and he became in his last decades a familiar late-night television guest, a large bearded raconteur whose celebrity had drifted loose from his work. He received the American Film Institute's Life Achievement Award in 1975. He died in Los Angeles on 10 October 1985, aged seventy, with several projects incomplete. One of them, The Other Side of the Wind, was finally assembled from his footage and released in 2018.

Whether he was destroyed by Hollywood or by his own inability to finish is a genuine argument with evidence on both sides, and the fairest answer is probably that both were true at once and that each fed the other.

sections.heading: Influence: What Later Filmmakers Took
sections.body:
The influence of Citizen Kane is easy to overstate and easy to underestimate at the same time, because it operated less by direct imitation than by expanding the sense of what was permitted.

The most concrete inheritance is in film noir and in the American thriller of the 1940s and 1950s. The high-contrast lighting with deep shadow, the wide-angle distortion, the ceilinged sets and oppressive low angles, and the fractured flashback structure with unreliable narration all became staples. Films such as Out of the Past, The Killers and Sunset Boulevard — which opens with its narrator already dead, a structural joke that Kane's opening death made available — carry the marks plainly. Toland's deep focus was picked up directly by William Wyler in The Best Years of Our Lives, also shot by Toland, where it is used for quieter dramatic purposes.

The generation of American directors who came up in the 1960s and 1970s treated the film as foundational. It was the standard text in the new university film programmes, which is itself significant: Kane became the film that taught filmmaking, partly because its techniques are unusually legible and can be pointed at in a lecture. Martin Scorsese, Steven Spielberg, Francis Ford Coppola, Paul Thomas Anderson and many others have acknowledged it, and specific echoes are traceable — the empty-mansion loneliness at the end of There Will Be Blood, the rise-and-corruption architecture of the Godfather films, the newsreel-pastiche openings that appear everywhere from Reds to superhero films.

The narrative device of a life reconstructed through conflicting testimony recurs constantly, in Kurosawa's Rashomon the following decade — arrived at independently, from a 1922 short story — and in a long line of subsequent films. The specific device of a search for the meaning of a dying man's last word has been parodied so often that the parodies now outnumber sincere uses, from a Peanuts strip to The Simpsons, whose Mr Burns is a sustained Kane joke complete with a lost childhood teddy bear.

There is a counter-argument worth taking seriously. Some historians, notably in the tradition of David Bordwell's work on classical Hollywood style, argue that Kane's techniques were largely already circulating — deep-focus staging in Renoir, expressionist lighting in the German cinema and in Universal horror, sound bridges in Rouben Mamoulian, ceilings in Ford — and that the film is better understood as a brilliant synthesis than as an origin. This is probably correct as film history and largely irrelevant as film influence, since it was through Kane that the synthesis reached the people who came after. A summary that survives contact with the evidence is that Citizen Kane invented very little and changed what a great many people thought was possible.

sections.heading: The Case Against, and What the Film Cannot Do
sections.body:
A guide that only praised the film would be poor criticism, and the objections raised over eighty years are substantial enough to state properly.

The most frequent charge is coldness. The film is an anatomy rather than a drama, and it holds its protagonist at arm's length by design: Kane is examined by witnesses rather than inhabited, and the structure guarantees that the audience never simply lives inside a scene with him without a frame around it. Viewers who want emotional identification often find the experience admirable rather than moving. Welles's own performance, magnificent in its middle-aged sequences, is arguably less convincing in the very young scenes, where a twenty-five-year-old plays a twenty-five-year-old with a strained heartiness.

The second charge is that the technique calls attention to itself. Every celebrated shot is celebrated partly because it announces its own cleverness, and there is a fair argument that this is a young man's film in the specific sense that it is constantly demonstrating. Welles's own later work, particularly Chimes at Midnight, is often held to be deeper and less exhibitionist, and Welles himself said something close to this.

The third is the treatment of women. Emily is a function of Kane's ambition, Susan is a victim of it, and Kane's mother is given one decisive scene and then nothing. The film's interest in its women is entirely instrumental. This was ordinary for 1941 and remains a real limitation for a work presented as the summit of the medium. The specific unfairness to Marion Davies compounds it.

The fourth objection is about the Rosebud device itself. Reducing a life to a childhood loss is a piece of popular psychology, and although the film arguably undercuts its own solution by having the reporter dismiss it, the closing image lands with an emphasis that is hard to read ironically. Welles called it dollar-book Freud and defended it as a gimmick that gave the audience something to hold; whether the ironic framing is strong enough to redeem the sentiment is a legitimate disagreement.

A final honest caveat concerns the canonical status itself. Polls of critics measure the opinions of a particular population at a particular time, and for most of the twentieth century that population was overwhelmingly male, Western, and trained on a narrow selection of what world cinema had produced. The 2022 result, in which a Belgian feminist film from 1975 displaced the American consensus choice, is best read not as a verdict that Kane got worse but as evidence that the earlier lists were measuring a smaller room. The film is one of a handful of indisputably major achievements in cinema; it is not obviously the single greatest, and the question may not be well posed.

sections.heading: How to Watch It, and What to Look For
sections.body:
Citizen Kane rewards deliberate attention more than most films, and a viewer who knows what to watch for will get considerably more from it. It runs 119 minutes, is in black and white, and is widely available in restored transfers; the picture entered a long copyright afterlife but remains commercially distributed, and modern digital restorations recover a great deal of shadow detail that older television prints lost.

On a first viewing, simply follow the story and let the structure work. Notice how much of the plot the newsreel gives away in the first ten minutes and how little that matters. Notice that the reporter Thompson is never shown clearly, usually being photographed from behind or in shadow, and consider why a film about the impossibility of knowing a man would deny a face to its investigator.

On a second viewing, watch the backgrounds. Because so much of the film is staged in depth, information is placed behind the ostensible subject: a figure in a doorway, a reflection, an object on a mantel. Look particularly at the snow globe, which appears at the start, again in Susan's boarding-house room long before the ending explains it, and in her bedroom at Xanadu. Watch the recurrence of glass, mirrors and framing devices — Kane is repeatedly seen through windows, in reflections, and in the famous shot walking between facing mirrors that multiply him into an infinite receding line of identical men.

Listen deliberately. Note where a line of dialogue crosses a cut into another time or place. Note how reverberation changes with the size of the room and how the last Xanadu scenes are recorded to sound cavernous. Note Herrmann's short motifs and how the Rosebud figure appears, usually on woodwind, at moments the characters do not recognise as significant.

Watch the physical scale of the compositions against Kane's fortunes. In his rising years he fills frames and is shot from below; in decline he is small within enormous spaces, dwarfed by a fireplace, a staircase or a stack of crates. The film states its argument through blocking as much as through dialogue.

For further reading, Robert L. Carringer's The Making of Citizen Kane is the standard scholarly account of the production and the script drafts. Peter Bogdanovich's book-length interview This Is Orson Welles gives Welles's own version, entertaining and not always reliable. Simon Callow's multi-volume biography is the fullest life. Pauline Kael's Raising Kane is worth reading as criticism provided its factual claims are treated with caution. Watching The Magnificent Ambersons, Touch of Evil and Chimes at Midnight afterwards is the best corrective to the impression that Welles made one film, and the best argument that the talent was real rather than a lucky accident of 1941.

guides.title: Film Noir
guides.summary: The origins, visual grammar, characters, industrial conditions and afterlife of film noir, and the long critical argument about whether it is a genre, a style, or a category invented later.

sections.heading: What Film Noir Is, and the Argument About Whether It Exists
sections.body: Film noir names a body of American films, made mostly between the early 1940s and the late 1950s, that share a set of preoccupations and a look: crime, moral compromise, sexual entanglement and fatalism, filmed in high-contrast black and white with deep shadows, oblique angles and rain-slicked night streets. The canonical examples are easy to list. The Maltese Falcon in 1941, Double Indemnity in 1944, Murder My Sweet and Laura in the same year, The Big Sleep in 1946, Out of the Past in 1947, The Asphalt Jungle in 1950, Kiss Me Deadly in 1955 and Touch of Evil in 1958, which is conventionally taken as the closing bracket. What is much harder is saying what the category actually is. Nobody who made these films called them film noir. The phrase was coined in Paris in 1946 by the critic Nino Frank, writing in the magazine L'Ecran francais about a batch of American pictures that reached French screens all at once after the wartime embargo lifted, and it borrowed its adjective from the Serie noire, the crime imprint Marcel Duhamel had launched at Gallimard the previous year. The term crossed back into English only gradually, becoming common in Anglophone criticism in the late 1960s and 1970s. So film noir is a category applied retrospectively, from outside, by critics of a different nationality, to films their makers understood as thrillers, melodramas, mysteries or simply pictures. That origin generates a genuine and unresolved critical dispute. Genres in Hollywood were normally industrial categories: the studio knew it was making a Western or a musical, advertised it as such, and the audience bought a ticket expecting one. Noir has no such production reality behind it. Some scholars, most forcefully Marc Vernet, argue the whole category is a French invention projected onto a heterogeneous body of work, and that many features supposedly unique to noir, the shadowed lighting, the flashback, the doomed narrator, appear in silent films and in 1930s pictures nobody calls noir. Others, including James Naremore in his 1998 study More Than Night, accept the point and argue the interesting question is not whether noir is real but how and why the idea was constructed, and what cultural work it has done since. The pragmatic position, and the one most working critics adopt, is that noir is best described as a style, a mood, or what the film scholar Paul Schrader in his influential 1972 essay called a tone, rather than a genre defined by content. A Western is defined by its setting; a musical by its numbers; noir by how it feels and how it looks. That is a looser definition than most genre labels carry, and it explains why every list of noir films differs from every other, with an agreed core of perhaps forty titles surrounded by a contested periphery of several hundred.

sections.heading: European Roots: Expressionism, Poetic Realism and the Emigres
sections.body: The look of American noir was largely imported, and by a specific and datable route. German cinema of the Weimar Republic had developed an expressionist visual language in which distorted sets, painted shadows and extreme chiaroscuro externalised psychological states. The Cabinet of Dr Caligari in 1920 is the extreme case, with shadows literally painted onto the flats, but the more durable influence came from films that used real light to the same end: F. W. Murnau's Nosferatu of 1922, Fritz Lang's Dr Mabuse films, and above all Lang's M of 1931, which combined an anxious modern city, a hunted murderer, a criminal underworld with its own courts, and a moral universe with no clean position anywhere in it. Alongside the visual tradition ran the Kammerspiel or chamber drama, and later the German street film, with its fallen women, sordid interiors and men destroyed by desire. France contributed poetic realism, the cycle of the mid and late 1930s associated with Marcel Carne and the writer Jacques Prevert, in films such as Le Quai des brumes in 1938 and Le Jour se leve in 1939, in which a working-class hero, usually played by Jean Gabin, is trapped by circumstance and fate in a foggy, doom-laden port or city, and dies. The mechanism by which these sensibilities reached Los Angeles was emigration. The rise of the Nazi party drove a large part of the German-speaking film industry to Hollywood, many of them Jewish, and the list of noir directors born in central Europe is remarkable: Fritz Lang, Billy Wilder, Robert Siodmak, Otto Preminger, Edgar G. Ulmer, Curtis Bernhardt, Max Ophuls, Fred Zinnemann, Anatole Litvak. Cinematographers followed, among them Karl Freund and Rudolph Mate, along with American-trained camera operators who had absorbed the same techniques. These were people who had personally experienced political catastrophe, exile, and the loss of a settled world, working in a foreign language in a country whose optimism they regarded with some scepticism. It would be too neat to explain noir's fatalism purely by biography, and plenty of noirs were made by American directors with no such history, among them John Huston, Nicholas Ray, Anthony Mann and Robert Aldrich. But the technical vocabulary, the willingness to underlight a face until half of it disappears, to shoot up at a ceiling, to let a set fall into darkness rather than filling it evenly with light, came into the American studio system with these people and their assistants, and it arrived at the exact moment when the stories being told needed it. One further European contribution is easy to overlook: a narrative attitude. Weimar cinema and poetic realism both treated fate as an active force rather than a metaphor, and both were comfortable with an ending in which the protagonist simply loses. American commercial cinema of the 1930s had generally required a redemptive resolution, and part of what makes early noir startling is the arrival of directors for whom an unredeemed ending was normal craft rather than transgression. Lang's American films, from Fury in 1936 through Scarlet Street in 1945 to The Big Heat in 1953, carry that assumption across intact.

sections.heading: Hardboiled Fiction and the Pulp Inheritance
sections.body: If the pictures came from Europe, the words came from American magazine fiction. The pulps were cheap periodicals printed on rough wood-pulp paper, and one of them, Black Mask, founded in 1920 and edited from 1926 to 1936 by Joseph Shaw, incubated a new kind of crime writing. The British detective story of the same years, in the hands of Agatha Christie and Dorothy L. Sayers, was a puzzle set in a stable society: a murder was an aberration, the detective an intellectual, and the solution restored order. The hardboiled story reversed every term. Crime was not an aberration but the ordinary condition of a corrupt city; the detective was a working man paid by the day who got beaten up regularly; and the solution, when it came, restored nothing. Dashiell Hammett, who had actually worked as a Pinkerton operative, wrote in a flat, behaviourist prose that reported what people did and said and refused access to their thoughts; Red Harvest in 1929 and The Maltese Falcon in 1930 established the form. Raymond Chandler, who came to fiction in his forties after losing an oil-company job, added a first-person voice of enormous stylistic personality, full of self-deprecating wit and extravagant simile, and a plot structure so loose that even he reportedly could not say who killed one of the characters in The Big Sleep. James M. Cain wrote a different and equally consequential strain: not detective stories at all but short, brutal first-person confessions by ordinary people who commit murder out of lust and greed, in The Postman Always Rings Twice of 1934 and Double Indemnity of 1936. Cornell Woolrich supplied paranoid nightmares of mistaken identity and running clocks, and W. R. Burnett wrote the criminal from the inside in Little Caesar and The Asphalt Jungle. Hollywood bought this material heavily in the 1940s because it was cheap, plentiful and pre-tested, and it hired the writers too, with mixed results: Chandler despised screenwriting while doing it brilliantly, co-writing Double Indemnity with Billy Wilder in a collaboration both men found unpleasant. What the fiction supplied beyond plots was a register, a way of speaking, hard, clipped, ironic, wounded, which is why noir dialogue is quotable in a way that most 1940s studio dialogue is not, and why the voice-over narration that became one of the form's signatures felt natural: it was the pulp first person, transposed to the soundtrack. The relationship between page and screen was never simple. Hollywood bought titles as often as it bought stories, and adaptations routinely discarded most of a novel's plot while keeping its atmosphere. The Maltese Falcon had already been filmed twice, in 1931 and, as a comedy called Satan Met a Lady, in 1936, before Huston's version simply followed Hammett's dialogue closely and proved that the material worked as written. Chandler's plots, by contrast, were routinely rebuilt. What survived adaptation reliably was neither plot nor theme but tone, which is itself an argument that noir is best understood as a matter of register rather than of content, and a reminder that the pulps supplied the cycle's sensibility more than its specific narratives.

sections.heading: Wartime and Postwar America: The Conditions on the Ground
sections.body: Noir emerged at a specific moment and the correspondences are hard to ignore, though causal claims about films reflecting a national mood should always be made carefully, since millions of people held many moods at once and the studios were chasing profit rather than expressing a zeitgeist. Still, the circumstances were unusual. The war removed roughly sixteen million American men from civilian life and brought several million women into industrial work, and both movements reversed sharply after 1945. Returning servicemen came back to jobs held by others, to wives who had run households alone for years, and in many cases with what was then called combat fatigue and is now recognised as post-traumatic stress. The theme of the veteran who cannot reintegrate runs through the period: The Blue Dahlia in 1946 gives its returning pilot a faithless wife and a murder charge, Crossfire in 1947 makes a demobilised soldier a killer motivated by antisemitism, and Act of Violence in 1948 turns on a wartime betrayal that follows both men home. The economy shifted too, from wartime scarcity to consumer abundance, and noir is full of characters destroyed by wanting things: an insurance salesman kills for money and a woman in Double Indemnity, and the plots of The Postman Always Rings Twice, Criss Cross and Scarlet Street turn on the same engine. Wartime propaganda had demanded clear moral lines, and there is a plausible case that the exhaustion of that demand made audiences receptive to films in which nobody is clean. The atomic bomb entered the imagery directly, most famously in the glowing box at the end of Kiss Me Deadly in 1955. From 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee investigations and the resulting blacklist affected the industry personally: Edward Dmytryk, who directed Murder My Sweet and Crossfire, and Adrian Scott, who produced them, were both among the Hollywood Ten, and Jules Dassin, director of Brute Force, The Naked City and Night and the City, was blacklisted and left for Europe, where he made Rififi in 1955. Some critics read the paranoia, entrapment and betrayal of late noir as a displaced account of that experience. Two cautions are worth keeping. First, many of these films were made before the events they supposedly reflect, since the first wave was in production in 1943 and 1944. Second, the same period produced enormously popular musicals, comedies and Westerns of complete moral clarity, and noir was never more than a minority of Hollywood output. It is better described as one available register within a large industry than as the voice of an era. The most defensible version of the social claim is narrower and more concrete: the war and its aftermath changed who was in the audience, what they had seen, and what they would tolerate on screen. An audience that had watched combat newsreels for four years was not going to be shocked by a shadowy killing, and an industry that had spent those years making films about moral certainty had exhausted a good deal of that vein. Noir filled a gap in the market as much as it expressed a mood.

sections.heading: The Visual Grammar: Low-Key Lighting and Unstable Space
sections.body: The classical Hollywood lighting scheme was three-point: a key light establishing the main modelling, a fill light softening the shadows the key created, and a backlight separating the subject from the background.
