The ratio between key and fill determines how deep the shadows go. Ordinary studio practice used a low ratio, perhaps two to one or four to one, giving an evenly and flatteringly lit scene. Noir works at high ratios, eight to one, sixteen to one, sometimes with the fill removed entirely so that the unlit side of a face goes to pure black. This is low-key lighting, and it is the single most recognisable element of the style. Its effect is not merely dark but selective: the frame contains islands of information surrounded by areas the audience cannot see into, which produces genuine unease because a viewer scans darkness for what might be in it. Practitioners built an extensive vocabulary on this foundation. Light thrown through Venetian blinds stripes a character with bars, a visual pun so common it became a cliche, but effective because it arrives before the plot has confirmed the trap. Hard, single-source light from below inverts the natural direction of illumination from the sky and reads as wrong at a level below conscious thought. Practical lights inside the frame, a desk lamp, a street lamp, a swinging bulb, motivate the extremity and make it feel observed rather than designed. Wet streets were sprayed by the crew because water reflects and turns a flat black road into a field of highlights. Smoke, fog and cigarette haze catch light beams and make them visible. Camera work reinforces this. Wide-angle lenses of 25mm or shorter exaggerate depth and distort faces in close-up; low camera positions include ceilings, which normal studio shooting avoided because the lights lived up there, and make the world loom. The canted or Dutch angle, tilting the horizon, was used sparingly by the best practitioners and heavily by the weaker ones. Deep focus, the technique associated with Gregg Toland's work on Citizen Kane in 1941, keeps foreground and distant background sharp at once so that a conversation and a threat can occupy the same shot. The technical means improved during the period: faster film stocks, better lenses and more sensitive emulsions made night location work possible, and by the late 1940s cinematographers such as John Alton, who shot T-Men, Raw Deal and The Big Combo and wrote the 1949 manual Painting with Light, were producing images with almost no fill at all. Alton was also fast and cheap, which mattered more to studios than aesthetics and is a large part of why the style spread. Composition reinforces the lighting. Noir framings crowd people against the edge of the frame or interpose objects, banisters, doorways, window frames, between camera and subject, so the viewer is always looking through something at somebody. Mirrors and reflections recur so often that they constitute a motif, splitting a character into two images and proposing duplicity before the plot confirms it.

sections.heading: Voice-Over, Flashback and the Shape of a Noir Narrative
sections.body: Noir films are frequently told out of order, and by someone who already knows how it ends. Double Indemnity opens with Walter Neff bleeding from a gunshot wound, speaking into a dictaphone to confess; the entire film is his account, so the audience watches a hundred minutes of scheming knowing from the first reel that it failed. Sunset Boulevard in 1950 goes further and is narrated by a man already floating dead in a swimming pool. D.O.A. in 1950 begins with its protagonist walking into a police station to report his own murder, having been given a slow-acting poison. Out of the Past hands its long central flashback to a man explaining his past to the woman he now wants to marry, and the telling seals his fate. The structural effect of this device is to convert suspense into dread. Conventional suspense asks whether the character will escape; noir's retrospective narration answers that question in advance and asks instead how the trap closed, which is a different and colder pleasure. It also produces an ironic distance between the narrating voice, which understands everything, and the acting figure on screen, who understands nothing, and that gap is where much of the genre's fatalism lives. The technique had practical origins as well as artistic ones. Adapting first-person pulp novels meant finding a way to carry the interior voice, and the wartime popularity of radio drama had trained audiences to accept narration. It also solved plot problems cheaply: a narrator can compress days into a sentence, which matters on a twenty-day shooting schedule. Not every noir uses it, and its overuse is one of the ways lesser films of the cycle betray themselves, since narration that merely describes what the image already shows is a confession of weak filmmaking. The best examples treat the voice as an unreliable character in its own right. In Laura, the narration begins with the critic Waldo Lydecker and then abandons him, a formal trick that undermines his authority. In The Lady from Shanghai in 1947, Orson Welles's Irish sailor narrates his own gullibility. In Detour, made in 1945, Al Roberts's account of two accidental deaths is so self-serving and so implausible that many viewers have read the whole film as the lie a guilty man tells himself, which is either a remarkable piece of subtlety from a six-day production or a happy accident, and criticism has never settled which. Music completes the apparatus. Noir scores drew on the same European emigre pool, and composers such as Miklos Rozsa, who scored Double Indemnity and The Killers, Franz Waxman, Bernard Herrmann and David Raksin, whose theme for Laura became a standard, brought a late-Romantic and modernist vocabulary of dissonance, unresolved harmony and low strings. Rozsa's use of the theremin in Spellbound and The Lost Weekend gave psychological disturbance an audible signature. By the mid-1950s jazz had begun to displace the orchestra, in Elmer Bernstein's score for The Man with the Golden Arm in 1955 and Miles Davis's improvised music for Louis Malle's Lift to the Scaffold in 1958.

sections.heading: The Noir Protagonist: Detective, Fall Guy and Doomed Man
sections.body: Noir protagonists come in several distinct varieties, and confusing them is one reason the category looks incoherent from a distance. The first is the private detective, inherited directly from the pulps: Sam Spade in The Maltese Falcon, Philip Marlowe in Murder My Sweet, The Big Sleep and Lady in the Lake, Mike Hammer in Kiss Me Deadly. This figure is a professional in a corrupt world who has one thing left, a private code, usually about not letting a client or a partner down, which he honours at real cost. He is competent, physically brave, verbally quick, and he survives; the detective film is the most optimistic corner of noir precisely because it retains a functioning moral agent. The second variety is the fall guy or ordinary man who steps once off the path. Walter Neff in Double Indemnity is a successful insurance salesman; Christopher Cross in Scarlet Street is a meek cashier and Sunday painter; Al Roberts in Detour is a nightclub pianist hitchhiking to see his girl. Each makes one decision, usually motivated by a woman or by money, and the film then documents the consequences with the patience of an engineer describing a structural failure. This is the strain that comes from James M. Cain, and its logic is closer to Greek tragedy than to crime fiction: the flaw is ordinary, the punishment is total, and the pleasure for an audience is the appalled recognition that any of us might do the same. The third variety is the man with no past or no memory, or with a past that will not stay buried: Jeff Bailey in Out of the Past, running a petrol station under a false name; the amnesiacs of Somewhere in the Night and Street of Chance; the doomed Swede at the start of The Killers, who simply lies in bed and waits for the men who have come to shoot him. What unites all three is a specific relation to agency. The classical Hollywood hero acts and the world responds. The noir protagonist acts and the world turns out to have been arranged already, so his actions accelerate a process rather than redirecting it. Physically these men are often shown as exhausted, sweating, drinking, dishevelled, filmed from above to diminish them, and the casting reflects it: Humphrey Bogart's lined face, Robert Mitchum's heavy-lidded fatalism, Dan Duryea's whine, Richard Widmark's giggle. Even the toughness is a performance under strain, and the films know it. A fourth figure deserves separate mention because it complicates the picture: the corrupt or compromised professional inside an institution. Force of Evil in 1948 gives its lawyer a numbers racket; The Big Heat sets a police sergeant against a department that has been bought; Touch of Evil turns on a celebrated detective who plants evidence because he believes he is always right; and Sweet Smell of Success builds a whole film out of a columnist and a press agent with no redeeming quality between them. These films locate the rot in systems rather than individuals, a more radical proposition than the private tragedies of the Cain strain.

sections.heading: The Femme Fatale and the Sexual Politics of the Cycle
sections.body: The single most discussed figure in noir is the woman who destroys the protagonist. Phyllis Dietrichson in Double Indemnity, played by Barbara Stanwyck in a deliberately cheap blonde wig that Wilder said made her look phoney on purpose, is the type: she initiates the murder plot, manipulates the man who executes it, and is planning his death before it is finished. Kathie Moffat in Out of the Past, Kitty March in Scarlet Street, Brigid O'Shaughnessy in The Maltese Falcon and Cora in The Postman Always Rings Twice are variations. The type has ancestors going back to Salome and Lilith and forward through the vamp of silent cinema, but the 1940s version has particular features. She is usually sexually knowing and financially motivated; her weapon is her intelligence rather than any supernatural allure; and she is very often the smartest person in the film. Feminist criticism from the 1970s onward, notably Janey Place's essay in the 1978 collection Women in Film Noir, made two observations that have shaped every discussion since. The first is that the femme fatale is a figure of anxiety about women's wartime independence: she has money, mobility, sexual autonomy and no interest in domesticity, precisely the traits American women acquired between 1941 and 1945 and were expected to surrender afterwards. The second is more surprising, that despite being punished in the final reel, these characters are granted an energy, wit and visual dominance that the films' good women never receive, so that the punishment reads as an imposed correction rather than a natural conclusion. Noir typically offers a second female role as a counterweight, the nurturing woman who represents an escape the hero does not take, such as Ann in Out of the Past or Keyes's implicit alternative in Double Indemnity, and the films are consistently less interested in her. It is worth resisting two simplifications. Not every noir has a femme fatale; many have no significant female character at all, and the heist and semi-documentary cycles are almost entirely male. And the type is not simply misogynist: Gilda in 1946 gives Rita Hayworth a character whose supposed treachery turns out to be performance, and In a Lonely Place in 1950 inverts the whole structure by making the man the danger and the woman the one who must escape, which is one reason it is now regarded as among the most durable films of the period. The visual treatment of these characters repays attention because it often contradicts the plot. The femme fatale is typically introduced in a framed, elevated or backlit shot that grants her the composition, and she frequently controls the conversation, the camera's attention and the flow of information for most of the running time. When the film disposes of her, it usually does so abruptly and in a flat, unglamorous setup. Whether one reads that as the Production Code's required correction imperfectly grafted onto a film that admired her, or as the whole point of a cautionary structure, is one of the genuinely open interpretive questions in noir criticism, and both readings can be defended from the same footage.

sections.heading: The City as Setting and as Character
sections.body: Noir is urban almost by definition, and the city it depicts is neither the gleaming metropolis of the 1930s musical nor a documented real place, but a compound: a downtown of cheap hotels, all-night diners, boxing gyms, apartment houses with communal telephones, nightclubs, bus terminals and rooming houses, connected by streets that are always wet and mostly empty. Los Angeles dominates because the studios were there and location work was cheap, and because Chandler had already written it as a place of sunlit corruption where the ugliness hides behind bougainvillea. New York supplies the vertical, crowded variant. San Francisco's hills and fog serve The Maltese Falcon and Dark Passage, and the eventual expansion of the cycle carried it to Chicago, New Orleans, Mexican border towns and, in Night and the City in 1950, a bombed and shabby London. Early noir was shot largely on studio backlots, which is not a limitation so much as a different aesthetic: a controlled set can be lit to an extremity no real street permits, and the artificiality contributes to the sense of a world slightly askew from the real one. From about 1947 a countervailing tendency emerged, driven partly by newsreel and wartime documentary technique and partly by cost. The Naked City in 1948 was shot substantially on New York streets with concealed cameras, and its closing narration, that there are eight million stories in the naked city, announced a documentary ambition. Call Northside 777 used real Chicago locations and a true case. This semi-documentary strain gave the cycle a second visual mode, grittier and flatter, which coexisted with the expressionist one for a decade. What both share is treating the city as an active force rather than a backdrop. Geography in noir is systematically disorienting: characters are lost in it, trapped by it, or hunted through it, and the films dwell on in-between spaces such as stairwells, corridors, lift cages, underpasses, docks and railway yards. The climactic chase through a subterranean space is close to a convention, from the sewers of The Third Man in 1949 to the oil derricks and drainage channels that recur in Los Angeles pictures. The city also functions morally. It is where the anonymity that permits reinvention also permits disappearance; where institutions, the police, the courts, the press, the unions, are shown as compromised more often than not; and where money is visibly the organising principle. Noir's small towns, when they appear, are not refuges but traps of another kind, as in Shadow of a Doubt or the deceptively pleasant Bridgeport of Out of the Past. The interiors are as characteristic as the streets. Noir apartments are rented, temporary and thinly furnished; offices are small, on upper floors, reached by a lift with an operator, with a name painted on frosted glass. Hotel rooms have a neon sign outside the window that flashes intermittently across the ceiling, a device so useful for animating a static shot that it became a signature. The cumulative effect is a world in which nobody owns anything and nobody is at home.

sections.heading: The Production Code and the Uses of Censorship
sections.body: Every American film of the classical period was made under the Motion Picture Production Code, a set of content rules adopted in 1930 and enforced with real teeth from 1934 by the Production Code Administration under Joseph Breen. No major studio would distribute a film without a certificate, so the Code functioned as prior restraint. Its provisions were specific and extensive: crime could not be presented sympathetically or in a way that inspired imitation, adultery could not be justified or made attractive, methods of crime could not be shown in instructive detail, and, most consequentially for noir, evil had to be punished. This looks like an insurmountable obstacle to a form built on adulterous murderers, and it partly explains why noir developed the techniques it did. Prohibition breeds indirection. If a sexual encounter cannot be shown, it is displaced onto dialogue of extraordinary innuendo, and the horse-racing conversation between Bogart and Bacall in The Big Sleep is the standard example of a scene that is entirely about sex while mentioning nothing. If violence cannot be depicted, it is implied by sound, shadow and reaction, which is frequently more disturbing than depiction. If a murder cannot go unpunished, the film supplies a punishment in the last two minutes, having spent the preceding ninety making the transgression compelling, and audiences are quite capable of noticing which part carried the conviction. The Code therefore did not prevent noir; arguably it shaped it into something more suggestive and more stylised than an unregulated cinema would have produced. There were casualties. The endings of numerous films were altered, source novels were sanitised in adaptation, and homosexuality could be indicated only by coding, which is why several noir villains carry markers of effeminacy or fastidiousness that read as insinuation today, an ugly convention that the Code's prohibition on so-called sex perversion effectively created. Individual battles were fought and sometimes won. Double Indemnity had been considered unfilmable for eight years because of Code objections before Wilder got it through in 1944, and its success opened the door for the rest of the cycle. The Code weakened through the 1950s under pressure from television, from foreign films exempt from its authority, from a 1952 Supreme Court decision extending First Amendment protection to motion pictures, and from producers such as Otto Preminger who released films without a certificate and profited. It was replaced by the ratings system in 1968, by which time the classical cycle was long over. Local and state censor boards added a second layer, since municipalities and several states operated their own review bodies with the power to cut a film for local exhibition, and foreign markets imposed a third: British, Australian and Scandinavian censors each had different rules, so studios sometimes shot alternative takes or endings. The practical consequence for anyone watching today is that surviving prints of the same title can differ materially, and restorations frequently reinstate footage removed for one territory. Touch of Evil exists in at least three distinct versions, including a 1998 re-edit assembled from a 58-page memo Welles wrote to the studio after seeing their cut.

sections.heading: Economics: B-Pictures, Cheapness and Why the Style Spread
sections.body: Understanding noir requires understanding how the films were financed, because the style is inseparable from the budget. From the 1930s American exhibition ran largely on the double bill: a cinema showed an A picture, rented on a percentage of the takings, and a B picture, rented for a flat fee, and the second feature had to be produced within a fixed low cost. B units at the major studios, and independent producers on the strip of small companies known as Poverty Row, worked to schedules of two to four weeks and budgets that in the 1940s might run from about 100,000 to 400,000 dollars, against several million for a prestige A picture. Low-key lighting is cheap. A set that is mostly in darkness does not need to be fully built or fully dressed, because the audience cannot see the corners. Shadow conceals the reuse of standing sets. Night shooting on location avoids the cost of exteriors altogether. A single hard source is faster to rig than a full three-point setup across a wide set, which saves the most expensive commodity on any production, which is time. Crime stories need no crowds, no period costume and no spectacle. Every economic pressure in the system therefore pushed second features toward exactly the aesthetic that critics later celebrated. The extreme case is Detour, made at Producers Releasing Corporation, one of the poorest of the Poverty Row outfits, directed by Edgar G. Ulmer in about six days for a reported budget under 100,000 dollars, using rear projection, fog to hide the absence of sets, and a running time of 68 minutes. It is now in the United States National Film Registry. The B context also granted freedom. Nobody at the top of a studio scrutinised a second feature closely, so downbeat endings, ambiguous morality and formal experiment could slip through in a picture that a prestige production would never have risked. This is why so many of the boldest noirs are cheap ones, and why the cycle's reputation rose so sharply once critics began watching films outside the prestige hierarchy. The same economics eventually killed it. The 1948 Paramount antitrust decision forced the studios to divest their cinema chains, which destroyed the guaranteed market for second features; television absorbed the audience for cheap black-and-white crime drama; and by the late 1950s the B unit as an institution had essentially ceased to exist. It would be wrong, though, to reduce noir to its budget. Several of the cycle's most admired films were expensive A pictures with major stars: Double Indemnity, Laura, The Big Sleep, Sunset Boulevard and Touch of Evil all had substantial resources behind them. What the B world contributed was not the style itself so much as the volume and the licence, producing hundreds of pictures a year in which the conventions could be tested, exaggerated and refined, and from which the prestige productions borrowed freely. The traffic went both ways: John Alton graduated from Poverty Row to MGM and won an Academy Award in 1952 for An American in Paris.

sections.heading: The Canon and the Chronology, 1940 to 1958
sections.body: Most accounts date the classical cycle from 1940 or 1941 to 1958, and it is useful to see it in phases, an approach Paul Schrader set out in 1972 and which has largely stuck. The opening is usually given to Stranger on the Third Floor in 1940, an RKO B picture with a startling expressionist nightmare sequence photographed by Nicholas Musuraca, or to The Maltese Falcon in 1941, John Huston's first film as director and the third adaptation of Hammett's novel, which established Bogart's screen persona. The first phase, roughly 1941 to 1946, is the studio-bound detective and doomed-lover period: Double Indemnity in 1944, Murder My Sweet and Laura the same year, Mildred Pierce and Detour in 1945, The Postman Always Rings Twice, The Big Sleep, The Killers and Gilda in 1946. The films are polished, dialogue-driven, often set in wealthy houses, and frequently structured around a flashback confession. The second phase, roughly 1947 to 1952, turns harder and more paranoid, moves outdoors, and admits the police procedural and the semi-documentary: Out of the Past and Crossfire in 1947, Force of Evil, The Naked City and Key Largo in 1948, White Heat and Gun Crazy in 1949 and 1950, The Asphalt Jungle, Sunset Boulevard, In a Lonely Place and Night and the City in 1950. This is generally regarded as the richest stretch. The third phase, roughly 1953 to 1958, is the most nihilistic and the most stylistically extreme, made under the shadow of television and the blacklist: The Big Heat in 1953, Kiss Me Deadly and The Big Combo in 1955, The Killing and Sweet Smell of Success in 1956 and 1957, and Touch of Evil in 1958, whose baroque three-minute opening crane shot is both a summation and, in retrospect, an epitaph. Any such list is arguable. Some critics include Citizen Kane for its lighting and structure, some exclude the gangster pictures on the grounds that they belong to an older genre, and some admit melodramas such as Leave Her to Heaven, which is in colour and about a marriage, on the grounds that its psychology is pure noir. That last case illustrates the general problem: if the definition rests on tone rather than content, no boundary can be drawn that everyone will accept. The size of the corpus is worth stating plainly, because it is often misrepresented. Reference works that adopt a generous definition list between three hundred and eight hundred American films for the classical period, against a total American output of roughly four hundred features a year through the 1940s, so noir on the widest reading accounts for something like five to ten per cent of production. On a strict reading it is far less. The impression that 1940s Hollywood was a shadowy place comes partly from the fact that the noirs have survived critical attention while the far more numerous comedies and programmers around them have not. Availability shapes the canon too: films that fell into the public domain, Detour and D.O.A. among them, circulated on cheap videotape for decades and became better known than contemporaries locked in studio vaults.

sections.heading: Variants and Subcycles Within the Classical Period
sections.body: The cycle is not homogeneous, and recognising its internal families removes much of the apparent confusion. The private-eye film adapts the detective pulps and keeps a functioning protagonist. The Cain-derived murder melodrama follows an ordinary person into a killing driven by lust and money. The heist or caper film assembles a crew, executes an elaborate robbery with near-documentary attention to procedure, and then watches human weakness dismantle the plan; The Asphalt Jungle in 1950 established the pattern, The Killing in 1956 refined it with a fractured chronology, and Rififi in 1955 exported it to France with a celebrated near-silent half-hour robbery sequence. The semi-documentary or police procedural, encouraged by the success of The House on 92nd Street in 1945, uses authoritative narration, real locations and institutional detail, and is politically the most conservative branch, since it restores the competence of the state. The gothic or paranoid woman's film, sometimes called the gaslight cycle after the 1944 film, places a wife in a house with a husband who may be trying to kill her, and includes Rebecca, Suspicion, Secret Beyond the Door and Sleep, My Love. The fugitive-couple film sends two lovers on the run to certain death, from You Only Live Once in 1937 through Gun Crazy in 1950 to They Live by Night. The prison and boxing pictures, Brute Force and Body and Soul, use enclosed institutions as images of a rigged system. There are noir Westerns, including Pursued in 1947 and Blood on the Moon, which import the lighting and the psychological darkness into an unexpected setting, and there are science-fiction and horror pictures that borrow the same visual approach. Colour complicates the taxonomy productively. Leave Her to Heaven in 1945, Niagara in 1953, Slightly Scarlet in 1956 and Party Girl in 1958 are shot in Technicolor and are noir by every criterion except monochrome, which is a useful reminder that the black-and-white photography, however iconic, is a strong tendency rather than a definition. Recognising these families also explains why newcomers sometimes find noir disappointing: someone who has been told the form is all shadows and doomed antiheroes and then watches a brisk procedural about federal agents will reasonably wonder what happened, when the answer is simply that they have met a different branch of the same tree. Two further subcycles are worth naming because they are often misfiled. The social-problem noir uses the crime frame to address a specific public issue: Crossfire tackles antisemitism, The Lawless and Border Incident deal with the treatment of Mexican and Mexican-American labour, and Odds Against Tomorrow in 1959 makes racial hatred the reason a robbery fails. These films come mostly from the political left of the industry and several of their makers were later blacklisted. The syndicate or expose picture, which flourished after the televised Kefauver Senate hearings on organised crime in 1950 and 1951 drew enormous audiences, treats crime as a corporation with an org chart, in titles such as The Enforcer, The Captive City and The Phenix City Story. Both branches point away from the existential fatalism usually taken as noir's essence and toward journalism.

sections.heading: Noir Beyond Hollywood
sections.body: Although the label was invented for American films, comparable cycles appeared elsewhere, and the traffic ran in both directions. Britain produced a substantial body of work often called British noir or spiv cinema, dealing with black marketeers, deserters and the shabbiness of postwar austerity: Brighton Rock in 1948 from the Graham Greene novel, They Made Me a Fugitive, Odd Man Out in 1947, and above all The Third Man in 1949, directed by Carol Reed and written by Greene, whose canted angles, rubble-strewn Vienna, zither score and sewer chase constitute one of the most complete realisations of the style anywhere. France, having named the thing, developed its own tradition, first through the crime films of the late 1940s and 1950s and then through Jean-Pierre Melville, whose Bob le flambeur in 1956, Le Doulos and Le Samourai in 1967 stripped the American model down to ritual, silence and a cold blue-grey palette. The French New Wave critics who became directors adored American B pictures and quoted them constantly: Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless in 1960 has its protagonist model himself on Bogart, and Francois Truffaut's Shoot the Piano Player adapts an American pulp novel by David Goodis. Japan produced a rich parallel cinema, from Akira Kurosawa's Drunken Angel in 1948 and Stray Dog in 1949, with their black markets and postwar desperation, to the stylised studio thrillers Nikkatsu turned out in the 1960s, including Seijun Suzuki's Tokyo Drifter and Branded to Kill, and later to the yakuza films of Kinji Fukasaku and Takeshi Kitano. Mexican cinema of the 1940s and 1950s developed a cabaretera and crime cycle sharing many of the same features, and Argentina, Brazil, India and Hong Kong all produced crime cinemas that critics have since read through the noir lens, sometimes illuminatingly and sometimes by force. Whether all of this constitutes one international phenomenon or several convergent responses to similar conditions, urban modernity, war, dislocation and the availability of the same cheap technology, is genuinely debatable, and the honest answer is probably some of both: shared circumstances producing shared preoccupations, plus direct imitation once American films began circulating again after 1945. Two specific channels of influence are documented rather than inferred. The first is personnel: blacklisted Americans working in Europe, above all Jules Dassin and Joseph Losey, carried studio technique directly into British and French production, and Losey's long English career, culminating in The Servant in 1963, transplanted a noir sensibility into a wholly different social milieu. The second is literary: American hardboiled fiction was translated and read voraciously abroad, and Duhamel's Serie noire imprint published Hammett, Chandler, Cain, Goodis and Jim Thompson in French, so that European directors were often adapting the same source material rather than imitating the films. Britain also had its own strong indigenous crime tradition through Greene and Patrick Hamilton, which is why British noir feels different in its class politics: American noir is about money and desire, while its British counterpart is frequently about class position and the shame of falling out of it, a distinction that survives into the television crime drama of both countries.

sections.heading: Neo-Noir: The Afterlife from 1967 Onward
sections.body: The classical cycle ended, but the style did not, and its revival is one of the clearest cases in cinema of a form returning as self-conscious homage. The transition begins in the late 1960s, when the collapse of the Production Code, the rise of a generation of film-school directors who had studied the older films, and the political disillusionment of the era converged. John Boorman's Point Blank in 1967 retells a hardboiled revenge novel in fractured, modernist form; Robert Altman's The Long Goodbye in 1973 transplants Marlowe into a sunlit, stoned Los Angeles where his code is an anachronism; and Roman Polanski's Chinatown in 1974, written by Robert Towne, is usually treated as the central neo-noir, taking the private-eye structure and pushing its pessimism past anything the Code would have permitted, with corruption that reaches the foundations of the city and cannot be touched. What distinguishes neo-noir from its model is the loss of innocence about the form. Classical noir was made by people solving practical problems; neo-noir is made by people who know they are making noir, and it therefore tends toward pastiche, quotation and reflexivity. It also has colour, explicit sex and violence, and no obligation to punish anyone. The strands that follow are varied: erotic thrillers such as Body Heat in 1981, which openly reworks Double Indemnity; the science-fiction hybrid of Blade Runner in 1982, which grafts noir lighting, narration and a detective plot onto a future Los Angeles and did more than any other single film to make the visual language ubiquitous; the regional and rural variants of Blood Simple in 1984 and the Coen brothers' later work; the period reconstruction of L.A. Confidential in 1997; the puzzle-box formalism of Memento in 2000, which literalises the unreliable narrator by running backwards; and a continuing stream including Drive, Nightcrawler and television series such as True Detective. The influence extends well past film into comics, video games, animation and advertising, to the point where a rain-lit street, a fedora and a saxophone constitute an instantly readable shorthand. That ubiquity is double-edged. It has kept the tradition alive and it has also reduced much of it to surface, since the visual signature is easy to copy while the moral seriousness underneath is not. A useful test when watching a modern film that presents itself as noir is to ask what it believes rather than what it looks like. Classical noir's fatalism was not decorative; it followed from a structure in which the protagonist's own choices tighten the trap, and the visual style existed to serve that structure. A film that supplies the shadows and the narration but allows its hero to win by being tougher than the villains has borrowed the surface and discarded the argument, which is why so much self-described noir registers as costume. The strongest neo-noirs update the mechanism rather than the wardrobe: Chinatown replaces individual doom with institutional impunity, Blade Runner asks whether the detective is himself the thing he hunts, and Memento makes memory the instrument of manipulation.

sections.heading: Critical Debates, Limits and How to Watch
sections.body: Noir criticism has passed through identifiable phases and each left useful tools and some overreach. The French founders, Raymond Borde and Etienne Chaumeton, whose Panorama du film noir americain appeared in 1955, proposed that the essential quality was a dreamlike disorientation, listing five characteristics: oneiric, strange, erotic, ambivalent and cruel. The 1970s brought two competing approaches, one broadly sociological, reading the films as symptoms of postwar anxiety, and one formalist, cataloguing lighting and composition; Schrader's essay does both. Feminist criticism from the late 1970s reoriented attention to the female figures. The 1990s brought scepticism about the category itself and a historicising turn, asking who invented the term and why. The most useful current position treats noir as what Naremore calls a discursive category, real in its effects on how films are made, marketed and watched, without pretending it existed as a production category at the time. Several honest limits are worth stating. The films' politics are mixed and often reactionary, particularly on gender and on race; Black characters appear rarely and usually as servants or musicians, and the cycle's much-praised social criticism has significant blind spots. The celebrated fatalism can shade into a self-pity that flatters the male protagonist as a victim of forces rather than an agent of harm. And a substantial fraction of the several hundred films the label now covers are simply mediocre programmers whose reputation rests on style rather than achievement. For a viewer starting out, a workable approach is to watch a small spread deliberately rather than a long list at random: one detective film, one Cain-style descent, one heist, one late nihilistic picture, and one non-American example, and to attend to three things while watching. Notice where the light comes from and what it conceals rather than what it shows. Notice who has knowledge and who does not, since noir plots are usually about the distribution of information. And notice the last five minutes separately from the rest, because the imposed resolution and the film's real convictions are frequently in open disagreement, and learning to see that gap is the most transferable skill the tradition teaches. Practical matters affect the experience more than they should. Presentation quality varies enormously, because many of these films were cheap productions whose original negatives were not preserved, and a muddy public-domain transfer destroys precisely the thing the films were best at, since detail in the shadows is the whole point and a poor copy turns modelled darkness into flat black. Where a restored print or a well-transferred edition exists it is worth seeking out. Aspect ratio matters too: films made before about 1953 were composed for the roughly four-by-three Academy ratio, and versions cropped to fill a widescreen television destroy compositions built around vertical space. Finally, it is worth remembering that these were popular entertainments watched by ordinary audiences on a Friday night, frequently as the second half of a double bill, not solemn art objects. They are, at their best, fast, funny, sexually alert and extremely well made, and the reverence around them can get in the way of noticing how entertaining they are.

guides.title: Early Film Movements: German Expressionism and Soviet Montage
guides.summary: How two silent-era movements, German Expressionism and Soviet montage, invented the visual and editing language of cinema, the films and theorists behind them, and their legacy in everything filmed since.

sections.heading: Two Revolutions in Seeing: Why These Movements Matter
sections.body: In the decade after the First World War, two defeated and convulsed societies produced the two most influential bodies of silent film ever made, and between them they invented most of the visual grammar that movies still speak. German Expressionism, flowering in Berlin between roughly 1919 and 1927, discovered that everything inside the film frame, the sets, the shadows, the makeup, the very architecture, could be bent to express a state of mind rather than to record a place. Soviet montage, developed in Moscow and Leningrad across the 1920s, discovered that the deepest power of cinema lies not inside the frame at all but between frames, in the cut, where two images collide and detonate a meaning neither contains alone. One movement is a theory of the shot; the other is a theory of the edit; together they mark the moment cinema stopped imitating theatre and photography and became an art with laws of its own. The claim is not antiquarian. Every horror film that lights a face from below, every thriller that leans its camera into a diagonal Dutch angle, every noir detective walking through venetian-blind shadows is drawing on the Expressionist toolkit, carried to Hollywood in the suitcases of émigrés fleeing Hitler. Every action sequence assembled from a hundred short shots, every reaction shot that makes you believe an actor is thinking something the actor never thought, every advertisement that cuts from a face to a product and lets your brain build the desire, is applying discoveries first formalized in the Kuleshov workshop and in Sergei Eisenstein's essays. Modern editing rhythm, the film school seminar, the idea that a cut is an idea, all descend from the Soviets; production design as psychology, the idea that a set can lie, hallucinate, or scream, descends from the Germans. The two movements also matter as a paired historical experiment. Both arose from catastrophe, Germany's military collapse and revolutionary chaos, Russia's revolution and civil war; both were incubated by unusual institutional hothouses, the giant UFA studio in Berlin and the nationalized Soviet film industry with the world's first film school; both were killed young, by the arrival of synchronized sound, by economics, and by the police states that rose over them, Nazism driving the German talent into exile and Stalinism strangling montage in favour of state-mandated Socialist Realism. Their brief lives concentrate a permanent question of media: what happens when artists, ideology, technology, and power share a small room. Studying them therefore pays three dividends at once. It trains the eye, because these films wear their techniques openly, making visible devices that later cinema learned to hide. It explains the family tree of genres, from horror through noir to the music video. And it offers a case study in how communication tools shape thought, since both movements believed, explicitly and in writing, that film could reorganize what an audience feels and believes, a claim the twentieth century went on to test at terrible scale. What follows traces each movement from its soil to its masterpieces to its afterlife.

sections.heading: Cinema Before 1919: The Ground They Grew From
sections.body: To measure what the Germans and Soviets changed, it helps to fix what cinema was when they found it. By the mid-1910s film was barely twenty years old as a public medium; the Lumiere brothers had projected to a paying Paris audience in December 1895, and Georges Melies had shown, in fantasies like A Trip to the Moon in 1902, that the camera could conjure rather than merely record. Most early films, though, were shot like theatre seen from a fixed middle seat: a static camera, full-figure framing, painted flat backdrops, and stories told in long unbroken takes with explanatory intertitles. The crucial pre-war advances in film language were largely American and largely practical. Edwin Porter's The Great Train Robbery in 1903 cut between parallel locations; by the early 1910s the director D. W. Griffith, working at the Biograph company, had systematized continuity editing, the invisible style that breaks a scene into establishing shot, medium shot, and close-up, matches the direction of movement and eyelines across cuts, and cross-cuts between simultaneous actions to build suspense. Griffith's feature The Birth of a Nation in 1915, as morally poisonous in content as it was influential in form, demonstrated that audiences would follow complex, feature-length narratives assembled from hundreds of shots, and Intolerance in 1916 interleaved four historical epochs in a single argument, a structure the young Soviet filmmakers would later study shot by shot; Lenin's government screened Intolerance widely, and the Moscow film school treated it as a textbook. The war itself rearranged the industry. European production collapsed while Hollywood industrialized, so by 1918 America supplied most of the world's screens, and any national cinema that wanted to exist had to answer Hollywood somehow. Germany answered with scale and art: the state-backed merger that created the giant UFA studio in 1917 gave Berlin production resources unique in Europe, and after the war a wartime import ban and hyperinflation sheltered German films from American competition while making exports lucrative. Russia answered with ideology and scarcity: the young Soviet state nationalized its film industry in August 1919, founded the Moscow film school the same year, and, starved of raw film stock by blockade and civil war, its students spent years re-editing existing footage and theorizing before they could shoot, a deprivation that turned out to be a laboratory. Two further inheritances shaped both movements. From Scandinavia, especially Danish and Swedish cinema, the Germans took moody naturalistic lighting and intimate psychological drama; directors like Victor Sjostrom showed that landscape and light could carry inner meaning. From the international avant-garde, Futurism, Cubism, abstract art, both movements took permission to treat the screen as composition rather than window. And from the war experience itself came the audiences: shell-shocked, bereaved, inflation-ruined publics in Germany hungry for shadowed fantasies, and a largely illiterate, multilingual Soviet population for whom silent images were the one mass medium that needed no reading. Cinema in 1919 was thus technically mature enough to be reinvented and culturally unsettled enough to permit it.

sections.heading: Weimar Germany: Defeat, Inflation, and the UFA Studio
sections.body: German Expressionist film is unimaginable outside the Weimar Republic, the democracy improvised on the ruins of the Kaiser's empire in November 1918 and battered from its first day. Germany had lost two million soldiers, its government had collapsed in mutiny and revolution, armed uprisings from left and right bled into street fighting through 1919 and 1920, and the Versailles treaty's reparations fed a currency collapse that became, by November 1923, one of history's most notorious hyperinflations, with the mark falling to over four trillion to the dollar and life savings evaporating between breakfast and dinner. Contemporary critics and later historians alike read the era's cinema through this trauma: films obsessed with tyrants, somnambulists, doubles, mad authority figures, and fate reflected a society that had watched authority lead it into an abyss and could no longer trust surfaces. The film historian Siegfried Kracauer pressed this reading furthest in his 1947 book From Caligari to Hitler, arguing that Weimar film revealed a collective psychology drifting toward submission to a strongman; the thesis is contested and certainly too neat, but the raw material for it, the parade of screen tyrants and sleepwalkers, is real. The industrial base for the movement was equally particular. Universum Film AG, UFA, had been created in December 1917 at the instigation of the military high command, merging major producers to make propaganda and boost German prestige; after the war it passed into private hands and became continental Europe's largest studio, with vast glasshouse stages at Babelsberg outside Berlin, first-rank technicians, and, in producer Erich Pommer, a figure willing to bankroll art as national branding. Pommer's Decla company, later folded into UFA, financed The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, and his logic was partly commercial: hyperinflation made German films absurdly cheap abroad, imports scarce at home, and a distinctive artistic style was something Hollywood could not copy, a market differentiation strategy that happened to fund masterpieces. The same economics built the studio-bound aesthetic. Shooting entirely indoors under controlled electric light was both an artistic choice and a practical one in a country where money lost value hourly and weather cost time; German cinematographers became the world's masters of artificial light because their industry lived in glass halls. Berlin itself supplied the sensibility: a city of cabarets, political assassination, jazz, war cripples, and avant-garde galleries, where Expressionist painting and theatre were already established high culture, so when cinema reached for artistic legitimacy it had a ready-made modernist vocabulary and an audience trained to read it. The republic's censorship was light by the standards of the age, which allowed the era's franker themes, madness, sexuality, crime, to reach the screen. It is worth holding on to the double nature of all this: Expressionist film was simultaneously a sincere scream from a wounded culture and a deliberate export product of a sophisticated studio system, art and industry in one body, and its greatest works, Caligari, Nosferatu, Metropolis, carry both signatures at once.

sections.heading: Expressionism Before Film: Painting and Stage Roots
sections.body: The style that startled filmgoers in 1920 had been growing in German galleries and theatres for fifteen years, and knowing the parent movement clarifies what the films were doing. Expressionism in painting named the revolt, beginning around 1905, against both academic realism and Impressionism's optical delicacy: instead of rendering the world as the eye receives it, the Expressionists rendered inner experience, distorting form and intensifying colour until a canvas showed not a street but the anxiety of standing in it. Two groups anchored the movement. Die Brucke, the Bridge, founded in Dresden in 1905 by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and fellow architecture students, painted jagged, angular city scenes and figures with slashing brushwork and acid colour; Der Blaue Reiter, the Blue Rider, founded in Munich in 1911 around Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, pushed toward the spiritual and the abstract. Behind both stood older ancestors the movement claimed: El Greco's elongated saints, Grunewald's agonized crucifixion, and above all the Norwegian Edvard Munch, whose 1893 The Scream, a figure dissolving into a howling landscape, is practically a storyboard for the aesthetic. The graphic arts mattered as much as oil painting: the German woodcut tradition, revived by the Expressionists, produced stark black-and-white images of gouged diagonals and crushing contrast, and the look of Expressionist film, shot on monochrome stock, is in many ways the woodcut set in motion. Theatre carried the style toward performance. Expressionist playwrights like Georg Kaiser and Ernst Toller wrote station dramas in which an abstracted protagonist, the Son, the Cashier, moved through stylized episodes toward transformation, speaking in telegraphic ecstatic bursts; staging stripped sets to symbolic fragments, and directors, above all Max Reinhardt in Berlin, developed a lighting practice of sculpted beams and engulfing darkness that put a character's soul on the wall behind him. Reinhardt's companies were the finishing school of the film movement: Ernst Lubitsch, F. W. Murnau, Conrad Veidt, Emil Jannings, and many of the era's key actors and designers passed through his stages, learning that darkness is a building material. Acting under this doctrine abandoned naturalism for the gestural: the body as expressive diagram, movements slowed, angular, dance-like, a manner film would need since it had no voice to carry emotion. The intellectual mood completing the inheritance was a German Romantic and Gothic undertow, doubles and doppelgangers from E. T. A. Hoffmann's tales, fate and the uncanny from the ghost story tradition, plus a fashionable anxiety about technology, the city, and the crowd. When cinema adopted all this, it made one decisive addition the older arts could not: continuous movement through a distorted world. A painting shows one moment inside a deformed space; a film walks you through it for an hour, and the spectator's own viewpoint, gliding among the painted shadows, becomes the deformed thing. That is the specific novelty the film movement contributed, and why its borrowings from gallery and stage produced something neither could achieve.

sections.heading: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari: The Founding Shock
sections.body: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, premiered in Berlin in February 1920, is the film that made Expressionism cinematic fact, and almost everything about it repays close attention. The script, by Hans Janowitz and Carl Mayer, two ex-soldiers with bitter memories of wartime authority, told of Dr. Caligari, a fairground showman who exhibits Cesare, a somnambulist kept in a coffin-like cabinet, and who by night sends the sleeper out to murder; investigating students, an abducted heroine, and a final unmasking of Caligari as the director of an insane asylum completed a parable the writers intended plainly: authority hypnotizes the common man and commands him to kill. Director Robert Wiene, with producer Erich Pommer's blessing, added the device that still fuels seminar arguments, a framing story in which the hero Francis narrates the tale from what is revealed to be the asylum itself, recasting the entire plot as a madman's delusion and converting the writers' anti-authoritarian fable into, depending on your reading, a betrayal of it or a deeper irony; Kracauer famously argued the frame tamed a revolutionary script into reassurance, though surviving evidence suggests the frame was contemplated early, and the film's ending, with Caligari benignly promising a cure while the walls behind him still twist, is anything but reassuring. What made the film epochal was its design. Three artists of the Berlin Sturm group, Hermann Warm, Walter Reimann, and Walter Rohrig, built the world entirely in the studio as a painted hallucination: streets that lean like knife blades, windows shaped like screams, alleys that narrow into wedges, and, in the boldest stroke, light and shadow painted directly onto floors and walls, so that illumination itself is scenery and cannot be trusted. Warm's dictum, that films must be drawings brought to life, was executed literally. The actors were tuned to the sets: Werner Krauss's Caligari is a hunched spider in a top hat, and Conrad Veidt's Cesare, gliding along a wall in black tights and greasepaint, moves like a figure escaped from a Munch canvas; his awakening, eyes opening in extreme close-up, remains one of silent cinema's most unnerving images. Technically the film is almost primitive, a mostly static camera and theatrical tableaux, which proves the point of its influence: its revolution was mise-en-scene, the total design of what the frame contains, demonstrating that a film's world can be built from the inside of a mind outward. The gamble succeeded commercially as well as artistically, playing internationally, causing a sensation in Paris and New York, and branding German film as the world's art cinema; the phrase Caligarism entered criticism as a name for deliberate distortion. Its progeny divide into two lines: the direct imitations of painted-world stylization, which were few, expensive-looking, and soon exhausted, and the broader lesson, absorbed everywhere, that design, light, and architecture can carry psychology. One more legacy deserves note: Caligari established the horror film's deepest structure, the ambiguity between supernatural menace and mental collapse, a hinge on which the genre still swings.

sections.heading: The Expressionist Toolkit: Sets, Shadows, and Acting
sections.body: Expressionist films share a recognizable device kit, and each device has a mechanism, a reason it works on a viewer, worth spelling out. The foundation is stylized mise-en-scene: sets built or painted to externalize emotion, with verticals tilted, corridors tapered to force false perspective, doorways cut as jagged polygons, and furniture scaled wrongly so that a desk can dwarf a clerk, as it does to the point of satire in Caligari's asylum office. The mechanism is projection: deprived of a reliable world, the viewer reads the distortion as the character's inner state, doing the psychological work themselves. Second is chiaroscuro lighting, the painters' term for dramatic light-dark contrast: a single hard source raking a face from the side or below, pools of light in engulfing black, shadows thrown huge and sharp against walls. Low-key lighting of this kind was partly a Reinhardt stage inheritance and partly a technical achievement of UFA's electricians; its most famous emblem, the shadow of Nosferatu's vampire climbing a staircase, claws spreading across the wall, shows the trick's power, since the shadow, larger and stranger than the actor, is scarier than any makeup. Shadows in these films act: they arrive before characters, betray them, murder them, and in Arthur Robison's Warning Shadows of 1923 a whole plot is conducted by silhouette. Third, the camera itself learns to lie. Tilted framings, later nicknamed Dutch angles from Deutsch, put the horizon on a diagonal so the world literally loses its level; extreme low and high angles make tyrants tower and victims shrink; mirrors, multiple exposures, and in-camera superimpositions materialize doubles and hauntings, a specialty of cinematographers like Fritz Arno Wagner and Karl Freund. Fourth, performance is calibrated to the graphic scheme: gestural, slowed, angular acting, faces whitened with makeup, eyes ringed dark, so the actor reads as one more designed element; Max Schreck's rat-faced Count Orlok and Brigitte Helm's rigid, hip-swaying robot Maria in Metropolis are bodies turned into typography. Fifth, narrative architecture leans on frames, dreams, and unreliable minds, stories nested inside asylum testimony or fever, so the audience can never fully stabilize what it has seen. Sixth, the movement's themes recur so consistently they function as devices: the tyrant and the sleepwalker, the double or doppelganger who is the self's dark twin, fate arriving on schedule, the uncanny automaton, the city as labyrinth. A definitional honesty matters here: only a minority of Weimar films are Expressionist in the strict painted-set sense, and scholars often prefer broader labels for the era's output, but the toolkit above migrated far beyond the core films, into the Kammerspiel chamber dramas' brooding interiors, the street films' night cities, and eventually into ordinary genre grammar worldwide. The kit survives because each device is cheap in information and rich in feeling: a tilted camera costs nothing, a shadow costs one lamp, and both tell the audience, faster than dialogue ever could, that the world on screen is wrong in some way that matters.

sections.heading: Nosferatu, Murnau, and the Unchained Camera
sections.body: Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau was the movement's poet, and his career shows Expressionism evolving from painted artifice toward something subtler and more durable. Nosferatu, a Symphony of Horror, released in 1922, was an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula, names changed but skeleton intact; Stoker's widow sued the tiny Prana Film company, won, and a court ordered the negative and prints destroyed, the production company dissolving into bankruptcy, and the film survives only because copies had already scattered abroad, one of cinema history's nearest misses. Artistically Nosferatu broke the Caligari mold in a decisive way: Murnau shot much of it on location, in the Baltic town of Wismar, the Carpathian-standing High Tatras, and real forests and seas, and let nature itself carry the dread. Sped-up single-frame carriage rides, negative-image forests flashing white on black, and the vampire's stiff, inhuman rising from his coffin, hinged upright like a plank, showed trick photography serving terror; hard daylight, withering the Count at dawn, invented the now-universal rule that sunlight kills vampires, which is Murnau's addition, not Stoker's. Max Schreck's Orlok, bald, rat-toothed, fingers lengthening across the film as his hunger grows, remains the least romantic and most parasitic screen vampire, plague rats flowing from his ship in an image tuned to a Germany that remembered 1918's influenza dead. The film demonstrated that Expressionism did not require painted sets, only an eye that could find the uncanny inside the real, a discovery that made the style exportable to every budget. Two years later Murnau completed the other half of the lesson with The Last Laugh, in German Der letzte Mann, 1924, written by Carl Mayer and photographed by Karl Freund at UFA: the story, a grand hotel doorman, played by Emil Jannings, destroyed by demotion to washroom attendant when his gold-braided uniform, his entire social self, is taken from him, is a chamber drama, not a fantasy, yet the film revolutionized technique with what contemporaries called the entfesselte Kamera, the unchained camera. Freund strapped the camera to his chest, sent it down a wire from a courtyard window, floated it drunkenly through a wedding party for a subjective hangover, and rode it in an elevator through the hotel lobby, making camera movement itself the narrator of a man's inner collapse; the film managed, save one ironic title introducing its imposed happy ending, to dispense with intertitles entirely, proving pictures alone could carry a feature. The pairing of these two films maps the movement's real bequest: from Nosferatu, location shooting charged with menace and the horror film's core iconography; from The Last Laugh, the mobile, subjective camera and the ambition of pure visual storytelling. Murnau himself was carried to Hollywood on their reputation, where Sunrise, made for Fox in 1927 with German craft and American money, won at the first Academy Awards and transmitted the whole toolkit into the American mainstream; he died in a car crash in 1931, aged forty-two, the movement's great lost continuation.

sections.heading: Fritz Lang: Destiny, Mabuse, and Metropolis
sections.body: Fritz Lang, Viennese, trained as a painter, wounded in the war, became the Weimar cinema's grand architect, the director in whom Expressionism scaled up into spectacle and fused with technology, crime, and myth. His breakthrough, Destiny, in German Der mude Tod, the Weary Death, 1921, staged a young woman's bargaining with a somber, exhausted Death across three exotic episodes, its images, a wall of candles each a human life, a vast featureless wall pierced by a Gothic arch, becoming immediate icons; Luis Bunuel and Alfred Hitchcock both named it a conversion experience, and Douglas Fairbanks bought the American rights partly to delay it while borrowing its flying-carpet trick for The Thief of Bagdad. Dr. Mabuse, the Gambler, 1922, four and a half hours across two parts, gave Weimar its definitive tyrant for the inflation age: a criminal mastermind of disguises who manipulates the stock exchange, hypnotizes victims at the card table, and treats society itself as a game board, the film cutting a documentary cross-section through nightclubs, seances, and speculators' offices; Lang and his co-writer wife Thea von Harbou explicitly framed Mabuse as a portrait of the era, and when the Nazis rose Lang answered with The Testament of Dr. Mabuse in 1933, putting Nazi-flavoured slogans in the madman's mouth, and the film was promptly banned. Die Nibelungen, 1924, a two-part national epic of Siegfried and Kriemhild's revenge, built geometric monumental forests and courts entirely in the studio, its dragon a seventeen-metre mechanical puppet, its compositions, human figures arranged as ornament in stone architecture, a style whose kinship with later fascist mass aesthetics has been uncomfortably noted, not least because Hitler and Goebbels admired the film. Metropolis, 1927, capped the movement's ambition and nearly bankrupted UFA: the most expensive silent film yet made in Europe, roughly five million reichsmarks, seventeen months of shooting, some thirty-six thousand extras by studio arithmetic, and effects supervisor Eugen Schufftan's mirror process, which married live actors to miniature cityscapes in-camera, a technique used for decades after under his name. Its future city stacks pleasure gardens for the elite above subterranean machine halls where workers march in ranks to feed furnaces that Freder, the ruler's son, hallucinates as Moloch devouring men; the inventor Rotwang's gleaming robot, given the saintly organizer Maria's face to incite the workers to self-destruction, produced in Brigitte Helm's double performance the century's defining machine-woman, ancestor of every android since. The plot's famous moral, the heart must mediate between head and hands, was thin even to contemporaries, H. G. Wells called the film silly, and von Harbou's politics drifted toward the Nazis while Lang, part-Jewish by descent, left; the film was cut savagely for export, and its full length was only substantially recovered when a nearly complete print surfaced in Buenos Aires in 2008. Yet as image-making, the flooding workers' city, the robot's birth in rings of light, the skyline of stacked traffic, Metropolis remains the source-code of screen science fiction, cited by Blade Runner, Star Wars, and every futurist skyline since.

sections.heading: Revolutionary Russia: Film as a Weapon
sections.body: Soviet montage grew from conditions almost opposite to Germany's: not a rich studio seeking export prestige but a besieged revolutionary state that decided cinema was a weapon and then, for a while, gave its young radicals the keys. The Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917 over an empire that was largely rural, multilingual, and only partly literate, and film's advantage was obvious: a silent moving picture needs no reading and speaks every language at once. Lenin's remark to his education commissar Anatoly Lunacharsky in 1922, that of all the arts, for us the cinema is the most important, became the industry's founding scripture. The state nationalized film production and distribution by decree on 27 August 1919, a date the Soviet Union thereafter celebrated as Cinema Day, and in the same year founded the Moscow State Film School, later famous as VGIK, the first film school in the world, initially teaching with almost no film stock at all. That scarcity was formative. Blockaded and consumed by civil war between 1918 and 1921, the country had barely any raw negative; students staged and restaged scenes without shooting them, and their teacher Lev Kuleshov ran what became known as films without film, while the one abundant resource was existing footage, newsreels, pre-revolutionary features, imported prints, which young editors learned to take apart and reassemble. Montage theory, the doctrine that meaning is manufactured in the cutting room, was thus partly a virtue made of poverty: a generation learned cinema as re-editing before it ever learned it as shooting. Agitation infrastructure pushed the same direction. During the civil war the government ran agit-trains and an agit-steamer, painted carriages carrying printing presses, speakers, and projection equipment to the front and the villages, showing short punchy agitki to audiences who had never seen a film; efficiency of effect per metre of celluloid was a military requirement before it was an aesthetic. When the fighting ended and the New Economic Policy of 1921 revived a semi-market economy, Soviet screens filled, awkwardly for the ideologues, with profitable Hollywood imports, Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks drew Moscow crowds the local product could not, and the montage filmmakers consciously studied the American style, above all Griffith's Intolerance, admired for its editing and cross-cutting even as its politics were dismissed. The young theorists concluded that American editing was fast but mindless, continuity without argument, and set out to build on its rhythmic power a cinema that would not merely tell stories but think, producing concepts in the viewer's head by collision of images. The state establishment, meanwhile, wanted anniversary spectacles and legible propaganda, and the space between those demands, radical formal experiment justified as revolutionary persuasion, is exactly where the masterpieces of 1925 to 1929 were made, on commissions for the twentieth anniversary of the 1905 revolution and the tenth of 1917. The arrangement was always unstable, geniuses funded by a censor, and it lasted roughly one decade.

sections.heading: The Kuleshov Effect: Meaning Made by Cutting
sections.body: The theoretical cornerstone of the whole Soviet edifice is an experiment so simple it can be described in a sentence and so consequential that every film school still teaches it. Around 1921 to 1922, Lev Kuleshov, still in his early twenties and running his workshop at the Moscow film school, took a piece of existing footage of the pre-revolutionary matinee idol Ivan Mosjoukine, a close-up chosen precisely because the face was calm and expressionless, and spliced the identical shot against three different second shots: a bowl of soup on a table, a child's body in a coffin, and, in the usual telling, a woman on a divan. Audiences shown the three sequences reportedly marvelled at the actor's range, the pensive hunger with which he regarded the soup, his heavy grief before the coffin, his desire for the woman, never realizing the face was literally the same strip of film three times. The original materials are lost and the experiment's details survive mainly through later retellings by Kuleshov and his student Vsevolod Pudovkin, with variations in what the paired shots were, so the story has a whiff of legend and modern replications produce measurable but modest effects; the honest summary is that the anecdote may be polished but the underlying phenomenon is real and robust. What the effect demonstrates has two layers. First, juxtaposition creates meaning that neither shot contains: the emotion is not photographed, it is inferred, assembled by the spectator from the collision of face and object. Second, and more radical, the viewer does the work automatically and attributes the result to the screen, experiencing their own inference as the actor's performance. Film meaning, Kuleshov concluded, lives not in the shot but in the sequence of shots; the shot is a brick, the edit is the building. His workshop pushed the principle further with creative geography, cutting together a man walking in one Moscow street, a woman in another, a Washington building from a newsreel, and a staircase somewhere else entirely into one continuous apparent place and meeting, and with experiments assembling an ideal screen woman from the lips, legs, back, and eyes of different actresses, montage constructing a person who never existed. The practical consequences radiate in every direction. All reaction shots work by Kuleshov's mechanism: the cutaway to a listener manufactures attention or doubt regardless of what the listener was thinking when photographed, which is why editors can perform an actor's best performance for them, and why documentary editing carries heavy ethical freight, since cutting an interviewee's neutral face against chosen imagery can fabricate attitudes wholesale. Advertising is applied Kuleshov, product spliced against desirable life until the desire transfers. Kuleshov himself, ironically, was a classicist who admired American continuity and wanted montage efficient rather than obtrusive, and his own best film, the 1924 comedy The Extraordinary Adventures of Mr. West in the Land of the Bolsheviks, is a nimble satire, not a manifesto. But his students took the brick-and-building doctrine in opposite directions, Pudovkin toward smooth emotional masonry, Eisenstein toward deliberate collision, and that argument built the movement.

sections.heading: Eisenstein's Montage: Collision and the Five Methods
sections.body: Sergei Eisenstein, born in Riga in 1898, an engineer's son trained in civil engineering before revolution and theatre claimed him, turned the Kuleshov insight into the most ambitious aesthetic theory cinema has produced. His starting axiom, announced in the 1923 essay The Montage of Attractions written for the journal LEF while he still worked in agitprop theatre, was that a work of art is a machine for producing effects in an audience, to be engineered from calculated shocks, attractions, rather than from story logic. Transferred to film, this became his famous quarrel with his fellow student Pudovkin: where Pudovkin described montage as linkage, shots laid like bricks toward an emotional sum, Eisenstein insisted montage is collision, meaning born from the conflict of two adjacent shots, as a spark jumps a gap; he liked the analogy of the Japanese ideogram, where the characters for dog and mouth combine to mean bark, two concrete things colliding into an abstraction. Conflict, for Eisenstein, operated inside the frame as well as between frames, conflict of graphic directions, of scales, of light values, of volumes, and the editor's task was to orchestrate all these conflicts at once. In his 1929 essay Methods of Montage he systematized a ladder of five types. Metric montage cuts by the absolute length of the pieces, a tempo imposed regardless of content, accelerating like a drumbeat. Rhythmic montage cuts by content-in-motion, the movement inside the shots against their lengths, the Odessa steps' soldiers' boots against fleeing crowds being his own exhibit. Tonal montage organizes by the emotional tone or dominant of shots, fog, light, mourning, as in the harbour lament of Potemkin. Overtonal montage lets all the stimuli of the shots resonate together, a totality he compared to the overtones of a chord. Intellectual montage, the summit and his obsession, cuts to produce a concept: in October, 1928, his film for the revolution's tenth anniversary, Kerensky climbs the same palace staircase over and over while titles list ever-grander ranks, ambition mocked by repetition, and a preening mechanical peacock intercuts with him; gods of many cultures descend in sequence from ornate Christ to primitive idol, an essay arguing the concept of god is constructed, conducted entirely in images. Eisenstein dreamed of filming Marx's Capital by such means. The theory has known limits, which he half-acknowledged: intellectual montage strains against narrative absorption, October baffled much of its audience, and the method suits argument better than character, which is why his people are types, the word he used, cast for physiognomy from non-actors, faces as legible as posters. But the core discovery, that the cut is a semantic operator, that A spliced to B asserts something about A and B, underwrites the entire modern grammar of cinema, from match cuts that equate a bone and a spaceship to political attack ads that need only place two images side by side. He wrote it all down, hundreds of essays later collected in Film Form and The Film Sense, making him not just the movement's director but its enduring professor.

sections.heading: Battleship Potemkin and the Odessa Steps
sections.body: Battleship Potemkin, made in 1925 when Eisenstein was twenty-seven, is the movement's masterpiece and remains, a century on, a set text in virtually every film school on earth. Commissioned for the twentieth anniversary of the 1905 revolution, the film compresses that year into a single episode, the mutiny of the battleship Potemkin of the Black Sea fleet, and structures it in five acts like a classical tragedy: the sailors' fury over maggot-riddled meat dismissed by the ship's doctor; the mutiny on the quarterdeck as marines refuse the order to shoot their comrades under a tarpaulin, and the leader Vakulinchuk dies; the mourning in Odessa harbour, where his body lies in a tent on the pier and the city's grief hardens into solidarity; the massacre on the harbour steps; and the fleet rendezvous, guns trained, that lets the Potemkin pass untouched, brother refusing to fire on brother. Eisenstein shot on location in Odessa with his lifelong cameraman Eduard Tisse, casting largely by typage, faces chosen for what they instantly signify, workers, priest, officer class, and cut the film at ferocious speed to a length of roughly 1,300 shots in about seventy-five minutes, several times the shot count of a typical contemporary feature. The fourth act, the Odessa Steps sequence, is the most analysed passage in film history. Tsarist soldiers in a machine-like line descend the monumental harbour staircase firing into the crowd, and Eisenstein builds the horror by systematic collision: the geometric rank of boots and rifles against the disorder of fleeing bodies; long shots of the whole staircase against sudden intimate close-ups, a student's spectacles, a mother's open mouth; downward flight against a lone mother climbing upward into the guns carrying her shot child; and, at the climax, a wounded mother falling against the baby carriage she has been shielding, which tips over the lip of the steps and bounces down through the slaughter, an innocent object carrying the sequence's whole terror. Screen time dilates far beyond real time, the descent lasting minutes that a real staircase would consume in seconds, because emotional duration, not clock duration, governs the cut. Three marble lions, sleeping, waking, rearing, cut together as one creature, make even the stones rise in outrage, intellectual montage in a single flourish. The massacre itself is invention, no such single event occurred on the steps, though tsarist troops did kill hundreds across Odessa in 1905; the sequence has been so persuasive that histories have had to correct the record it planted, the sharpest demonstration on film of montage's power to manufacture memory. The film's afterlife proves the point from every side: banned for decades in various Western countries as inflammatory propaganda, admired professionally even by its enemies, Goebbels held it up as the model propaganda film and demanded a Nazi equivalent, voted the greatest film ever made at the 1958 Brussels world exposition poll, and pillaged affectionately ever since, most famously in the pram bouncing down the station steps of Brian De Palma's The Untouchables in 1987.

sections.heading: Pudovkin, Vertov, and Dovzhenko: Rival Paths
sections.body: Montage was never one doctrine but a family argument, and the movement's breadth is best seen through Eisenstein's three great contemporaries. Vsevolod Pudovkin, Kuleshov's star pupil, a trained chemist who came to film after war imprisonment, practised montage as linkage: shots as bricks building a continuous emotional structure, the spectator carried rather than jolted. His trilogy of features, Mother in 1926, from Gorky's novel, The End of St. Petersburg in 1927, and Storm Over Asia in 1928, centres on individual protagonists who awaken politically, a mother who takes up her dead son's cause, a peasant lad radicalized in the capital, a Mongolian trapper who rises against colonial masters, and his cutting serves their inner arcs with lyric interpolations, the famous ice-break flowing beside the prisoners' march in Mother equating spring thaw with rising revolt. Pudovkin's textbooks, Film Technique and Film Acting, translated early and widely, taught the world a workable, humane montage compatible with stars and stories, which is why his influence on mainstream narrative filmmaking arguably exceeded Eisenstein's. Dziga Vertov, born Denis Kaufman, came from newsreel, editing the civil-war Kino-Nedelia reels and then the Kino-Pravda series through the early twenties, and he despised fiction outright: acted cinema, he wrote in the manifestos of his kinoks group, was an opiate, and the future belonged to the kino-eye, the camera as an instrument that sees better than the human eye, catching life unawares.
